recipes.name: Split a crate into file modules with `mod name;` and share internals via pub(crate) / pub(super), not pub
recipes.what: A package holds at most one library crate plus any number of binaries; each crate is a module tree in which `mod name;` loads name.rs (or name/mod.rs, never both), and privacy is per module, so pub(crate) and pub(super) say exactly who may use an item.
recipes.how: Crate roots: src/lib.rs (the library, named after the package) and src/main.rs or src/bin/*.rs (binaries). In lib.rs, `mod rapier_law;` loads src/rapier_law.rs; inside that non-mod-rs file, `mod name;` loads src/rapier_law/name.rs. A private item is visible to its module and that module's descendants; `pub(super)` widens it to the parent module, `pub(crate)` to the whole crate, `pub(in crate::a)` to a named ancestor (from 2018 on the path must start with crate, self or super), and `pub(self)` is the same as private. Other files reach an item with `use crate::path::Item`. Compiler proof on 1.98.1: calling a pub(super) fn from the crate root is E0603 `function only_outer is private`; `mod rapier_law;` with no file is E0583 `file not found for module rapier_law`, whose help names both rapier_law.rs and rapier_law\mod.rs.
recipes.rust_version: any; pub(in path) path rules as of edition 2018; measured on rustc 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: A module is declared once with `mod`; writing `mod x;` a second time in another file is the mistake E0583's note points at (import it with `use crate::...` instead). Having both util.rs and util/mod.rs is an error; the mod.rs form was the only nested layout before rustc 1.30 and is still accepted, but the Reference encourages name.rs. `pub` does not export anything from a wasm cdylib (measured: a module with a plain `pub fn` and a `pub(crate) fn` beside a `#[no_mangle] pub extern "C" fn api` exported only `memory` and `api`), so in a crate nobody links as Rust, bare `pub` only blurs intent; pub(crate) says it. A `pub` item inside a private module is still unreachable from outside, because every ancestor module must be accessible too.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/lib.rs declares `mod rapier_law;` (solver/src/rapier_law.rs) and shares its ABI constants (`pub(crate) const BODY_STRIDE = 17`, HX..DRIVEN, `COLLIDER_STRIDE = 10`) and `pub(crate) static mut BODIES / COLLIDERS`, which rapier_law.rs imports with `use crate::{BODIES, BODY_STRIDE, COLLIDERS, ...}`; rapier_law.rs keeps its own `pub(crate) static mut HEIGHTS`. That is the right shape for a cdylib with no Rust consumers. T2's `restore_ptr` input buffer and `solver_restore` fit beside the snapshot code in rapier_law.rs with the same pub(crate) scope; if that file is split, `mod snapshot;` inside it loads solver/src/rapier_law/snapshot.rs.
recipes.verify_note: Reproduced E0603 and E0583 verbatim on rustc 1.98.1. Reproduced the wasm gotcha myself: a cdylib with plain pub fn + pub(crate) fn beside #[no_mangle] api exported only memory,api.

recipes.name: Choose [lib] crate-type by who loads it: cdylib for the wasm module, rlib for Rust callers, staticlib for C
recipes.what: crate-type belongs to the library target (default "lib", the compiler-recommended Rust library); cdylib produces a system dynamic library for another language to load, which on wasm32-unknown-unknown is the .wasm module, while library dependencies are still compiled as Rust libraries whatever the root chooses.
recipes.how: `[lib] crate-type = ["cdylib"]` (an array; list several to get several outputs). Measured with cargo 1.98.1 on a scratch copy of the solver manifest and lock: si_solver compiled with `--crate-type cdylib` into target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/si_solver.wasm, while rapier3d_f64 compiled with `--crate-type lib --emit=dep-info,metadata,link` into deps/librapier3d_f64-<hash>.rlib plus .rmeta; across the whole graph the verbose log shows 45 `--crate-type lib` units, 4 proc-macro, 8 build-script bins and the one cdylib. A stub cdylib exported exactly `memory` and its one `#[no_mangle] pub extern "C"` function and imported nothing. Per the Reference: cdylib gives .so / .dylib / .dll on native hosts; staticlib bundles the crate and all upstream dependencies into .a (Linux, macOS, MinGW) or .lib (MSVC) and rustc never links to it; rlib is the intermediate that the compiler reads in later linkage. Measured: a package whose only crate-type is cdylib runs an in-crate `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` unit test (`1 passed`) but fails a tests/ integration test with E0433 `cannot find module or crate cdy`; `crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]` makes that integration test pass (test-side details are the testing lane's).
recipes.gotchas: "lib" is compiler-defined and may change; write "rlib" when the Rust-library form is what you need. crate-type can only be set for libraries and examples; bins, tests and benches are always bin. A package has at most one library target, so a second output shape is another entry in the same crate-type array or another package. Adding "rlib" is not free for a pinned artifact: on a scratch copy of the real solver source, `crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"]` (rustc gets `--crate-type cdylib --crate-type rlib`) changed si_solver.wasm's SHA-256 and size (1,524,412 -> 1,524,440 bytes) with the same flags on the same host. Choosing cdylib does not decide exports: only the unmangled extern functions (and memory) appear in the module.
recipes.engine_note: solver/Cargo.toml's `[lib] crate-type = ["cdylib"]` is why solver/build.mjs reads solver/target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/si_solver.wasm, with rapier3d-f64 and its tree linked in as rlibs. The pure helpers (js_min / js_max in lib.rs; canon, canon_quat, mix_f64 in rapier_law.rs) are private fns, so their native tests belong in in-crate #[cfg(test)] modules, which run under the cdylib-only crate-type (measured); a tests/ directory would need "rlib" plus pub helpers, and adding "rlib" moved the wasm digest in a measured build, so it would re-pin fixtures/solver.sha256 once. The host-binding phase (the law inside Godot, then Unreal) makes this choice again for a native triple: the same export compiles as a host cdylib (a .dll on this Windows rig) and as a staticlib (checks below).
recipes.verify_note: Rebuilt the real solver (rapier3d-f64 0.35.3) in scratch: adding rlib changed the wasm SHA-256, delta +28 bytes matching the recipe's claimed delta exactly; dep graph counts (45 lib/4 proc-macro/8 bin) matched exactly.

recipes.name: Read a bare `"0.35.3"` requirement as >=0.35.3, <0.36: commit Cargo.lock and build the artifact with --locked
recipes.what: A bare version requirement is a caret range (the left-most non-zero component is fixed), Cargo.lock holds the exact versions and wins while it can, and only --locked turns a lockfile that would change into an error; without it Cargo rewrites Cargo.lock and keeps building.
recipes.how: Syntax: "0.35.3" is "^0.35.3" := >=0.35.3, <0.36.0; "1.2.3" := >=1.2.3, <2.0.0; "0.0.3" := >=0.0.3, <0.0.4; "=0.35.3" is exact. Measured on cargo 1.98.1 with a dependency `foo = { path = "foo", version = "0.35.3" }` (Cargo checks a path dependency's version against the requirement): foo 0.35.9 locked; foo 0.36.0 failed `failed to select a version for the requirement foo = "^0.35.3"` / `candidate versions found which didn't match: 0.36.0`; with "=0.35.3", foo 0.35.9 failed the same way. After foo moved 0.35.9 -> 0.35.10: `cargo build --locked` stopped with `cannot update the lock file ... because --locked was passed to prevent this`; plain `cargo build` printed `Updating foo v0.35.9 (...) -> v0.35.10`, rewrote Cargo.lock and built; with Cargo.lock deleted, --locked failed `cannot create the lock file`. --offline restricts Cargo to crates already downloaded and may resolve differently; --frozen is --locked plus --offline (a --frozen release build of a scratch copy of the solver succeeded from the local cache).
recipes.gotchas: The lock pins only while the manifest agrees with it: edit Cargo.toml and a plain build re-resolves the changed part without asking. `cargo update` (or `cargo update rapier3d-f64`) moves requirements to the newest compatible versions, here any 0.35.x at or above 0.35.3. The old advice (commit Cargo.lock for binaries, not libraries) was replaced in August 2023 by 'do what is best for your project', and cargo new stopped ignoring the lockfile; the Cargo Book now says to commit it when in doubt. For a crate whose output bytes are pinned by a digest there is no doubt.
recipes.engine_note: solver/Cargo.toml's `rapier3d-f64 = { version = "0.35.3", ... }` admits any 0.35.x at or above 0.35.3; the committed solver/Cargo.lock (lockfile version 4, 61 packages) is what pins rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 and parry3d-f64 0.30.2, each with a checksum. solver/build.mjs spawns `cargo build --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` with no --locked, so CI's `node solver/build.mjs --check` would quietly re-resolve after a manifest edit and only a digest mismatch could notice. Add '--locked' to that argument list; write "=0.35.3" as well if even a deliberate `cargo update` must not move the physics crate.
recipes.verify_note: Reproduced all 4 measured cargo error/update messages word-for-word on 1.98.1: the ^0.35.3 and =0.35.3 'failed to select a version' rejections, --locked's 'cannot update'/'cannot create', and the plain-build auto-update line.

recipes.name: Assume a Cargo feature enabled by any dependent is on for all; audit with `cargo tree -e features -i <crate>`
recipes.what: Cargo compiles a dependency with the union of the features that every package selected for the build asks for (resolver 2 keeps build-dependencies, proc-macros and dev-dependencies apart), each passed to rustc as `--cfg feature="name"`, so `default-features = false` in one manifest does not keep defaults off when another dependent enables them.
recipes.how: Measured (cargo 1.98.1, resolver 2 workspace): core_c has `default = ["std"]`, `std`, `parallel`; member a depends on it with default-features = false, member b with features = ["parallel", "std"], and app uses both. `cargo run -p app` printed `a sees core_c mode=parallel std=true`; the verbose whole-workspace build compiled core_c once with `--cfg 'feature="default"' --cfg 'feature="parallel"' --cfg 'feature="std"'` (default is on because core_c is itself a selected member), while `cargo build -p a` compiled it with no feature cfgs. `cargo tree -p app -e features -i core_c` names the enabler (`core_c feature "parallel"` <- `b v0.1.0`). Optional deps: `extra = { path = "../extra", optional = true }` with `fast = ["dep:extra"]` removes the implicit feature, and `--features extra` failed `package a ... does not have feature extra` with a help line naming the dep: syntax; `"pkg?/feat"` turns a feature on only if something else enabled the optional dep. Resolver 2 (edition 2021 default) does not unify features into build-dependencies and proc-macros, into dev-dependencies unless a target needs them, or from platform-specific dependencies of targets not being built.
recipes.rust_version: any; dep: and ?/ syntax 1.60+; resolver 2 is the edition-2021 default; measured on cargo 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: Features must be additive: offer a `std` feature, never a `no_std` one. The set of packages built together changes the features (a whole-workspace build versus -p a). Every dependent must write default-features = false for the defaults to stay off. Resolver 2 may build one crate twice with different features; `cargo tree --duplicates` lists it.
recipes.engine_note: Measured on a scratch copy of solver/Cargo.toml and solver/Cargo.lock: `cargo tree -e features -i rapier3d-f64 --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --frozen` lists alloc, block-solver, default, dim3, enhanced-determinism, f64 and std (enhanced-determinism from si-solver, the rest through default) and no `parallel`; rapier3d_f64's rustc line carries exactly those seven `--cfg feature=` flags. Any crate later built in one graph with the solver (a host-binding crate in a shared workspace) that enables rapier's `parallel` turns it on for the solver's build as well, so that tree command is the guard whose output must never show `feature "parallel"` (wiring it into CI is the ci lane's).
recipes.verify_note: Built the exact 4-package workspace: printed 'a sees core_c mode=parallel std=true' verbatim; whole-ws build shows core_c getting default+parallel+std cfgs, -p a alone gets none; cargo tree -i named b as the enabler.

recipes.name: Set [profile.*] only in the root manifest, and remember config files and CARGO_PROFILE_* env vars override it
recipes.what: Cargo reads profiles only from the workspace root's Cargo.toml and applies them to every crate in the graph (per-package overrides aside), emits a rustc -C flag only where a setting differs from rustc's own default, and lets a [profile] table in .cargo/config.toml or a CARGO_PROFILE_<NAME>_<KEY> variable override the manifest.
recipes.how: Measured on cargo 1.98.1 (`cargo build -v`): the default release profile emits `-C opt-level=3 -C strip=debuginfo` (debug assertions and overflow checks are already off in rustc at opt-level above 0; lto = false emits nothing); release plus debug-assertions = true emits `-C debug-assertions=on -C overflow-checks=off`, because rustc otherwise derives overflow checks from debug assertions; release plus debug = true emits `-C debuginfo=2` and drops the strip; dev emits `-C debuginfo=2` only. A path dependency's own [profile.release] overflow-checks = true was ignored without a word (its `x + 1` wrapped); a workspace member's [profile] warns `profiles for the non root package will be ignored, specify profiles at the workspace root`. With the manifest at overflow-checks = false, both `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_OVERFLOW_CHECKS=true cargo run --release` and `[profile.release] overflow-checks = true` in .cargo/config.toml panicked `attempt to add with overflow` (exit 101). `[profile.release.package.dep1] panic = "abort"` is a manifest error, `panic may not be specified in a package profile` (lto and rpath are refused too). Override order: [profile.X.package.<name>] > [profile.X.package."*"] > [profile.X.build-override] > [profile.X] > built-in defaults.
recipes.rust_version: any; strip = "debuginfo" by default when no debuginfo is emitted since 1.77; measured on cargo 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: The profiles page still lists the strip default as "none", but since 1.77 a profile that emits no debuginfo gets strip = "debuginfo" (release announcement; measured `-C strip=debuginfo`): a default that changed once can change again. lto = false means thin local LTO, which rustc disables when codegen-units = 1 or opt-level = 0. panic is ignored by tests, benches, build scripts and proc macros, a test build forces dependencies to unwind, and if any crate in the graph uses abort, the final binary must use abort too. Incremental applies only to workspace members and path dependencies, and CARGO_INCREMENTAL overrides it.
recipes.engine_note: Measured on a scratch copy of the solver: si_solver compiles with `--crate-type cdylib -C opt-level=3 -C panic=abort -C embed-bitcode=no -C codegen-units=1 ... -C strip=debuginfo`, and rapier3d_f64 gets the same opt-level, panic and codegen-units, so solver/Cargo.toml's [profile.release] governs the whole law. Of its five keys only panic = "abort" and codegen-units = 1 change what Cargo emits; opt-level = 3, lto = false and overflow-checks = false restate defaults (useful as a record, silent on the command line). The unpinned settings that decide bytes are strip and debug; writing `debug = false` and `strip = "debuginfo"` would record today's choice (a suggestion, not measured). A [profile.release] in a builder's ~/.cargo/config.toml or a CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_* variable changes local bytes, which only the Linux CI digest catches.
recipes.verify_note: Reproduced Cargo's real rustc invocations on 1.98.1: default release emits -C opt-level=3 -C strip=debuginfo; +debug-assertions=true adds explicit -C overflow-checks=off; member [profile] warning text matched verbatim.

recipes.name: Share lock, target dir and lints across crates with [workspace.dependencies] and [workspace.lints]
recipes.what: Workspace members share one Cargo.lock and one target/ at the root, [profile], [patch] and [replace] count only in the root manifest, [workspace.dependencies] and [workspace.lints] are inherited with `workspace = true`, and a virtual workspace must name its resolver or it falls back to resolver 1.
recipes.how: Root: `[workspace] members = [...]`, `resolver = "2"` (or "3"), `[workspace.dependencies] core_c = { path = "core_c", default-features = false }`, `[workspace.lints.rust] unsafe_code = "forbid"`. Member: `core_c.workspace = true`, or `core_c = { workspace = true, features = ["parallel"] }` (features add to the workspace entry's), and `[lints] workspace = true`; [workspace.package] can share edition and rust-version. Measured on cargo 1.98.1: one Cargo.lock and one target/ at the root and none in members; a virtual root without resolver warned `virtual workspace defaulting to resolver = "1" despite one or more workspace members being on edition 2021 which implies resolver = "2"`; the inherited lint reached rustc as `--forbid=unsafe_code` and failed `usage of an unsafe block`. Registry dependencies compile with `--cap-lints allow` (seen on rapier3d_f64's rustc line), so [lints] polices only your own packages.
recipes.rust_version: workspace inheritance 1.64+; [lints] respected as of 1.74; measured on cargo 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: forbid cannot be relaxed in source: `#[allow(unsafe_code)]` under it is E0453 `allow(unsafe_code) incompatible with previous forbid`, while deny can be allowed item by item. A virtual workspace ignores its members' editions when picking the resolver. Members' [profile] tables are ignored with a warning. Invoked from the workspace root, Cargo does not read .cargo/config.toml files inside member directories.
recipes.engine_note: solver/ is a standalone package today, with its own Cargo.lock, target/ and .cargo/config.toml. If host-binding crates join it under a root workspace, three things move together: the lock and target/ go to the root (so build.mjs's solver/target/wasm32-unknown-unknown/release/si_solver.wasm path changes), solver/Cargo.toml's [profile.release] is ignored until it moves to the root manifest, and solver/.cargo/config.toml stops being read when cargo runs from the root, which leaves the relaxed-SIMD pin living only in build.mjs's RUSTFLAGS. The solver cannot take unsafe_code = "forbid" (its exports reach static mut buffers inside unsafe blocks, and forbid admits no local allow); deny with a local allow, or narrower lints, fit it.
recipes.verify_note: Reproduced the virtual-workspace resolver warning and the [workspace.lints] to --forbid=unsafe_code mapping verbatim on 1.98.1, incl. the unsafe-block rejection and E0453 under forbid.

recipes.name: Migrate a crate's edition with `cargo fix --edition`, then edit `edition` yourself, then rebuild and test
recipes.what: The edition is chosen per package (absent means 2015), crates of every edition link into one binary, and `cargo fix --edition` rewrites code toward the next edition but never changes the edition field and cannot fix everything.
recipes.how: Measured (cargo 1.98.1): a 2024 package using a 2015 dependency (no edition key) and a 2021 dependency built and ran, calling `old::r#async()` and `mid::r#gen()` through raw identifiers; `cargo build -v` showed `--edition=2024`, `--edition=2015`, `--edition=2021`. Built as the root, the package without an edition key warned `package.edition is unspecified, defaulting to 2015 while the latest is 2024`. Migrating a 2021 cdylib shaped like the solver's exports with `cargo fix --edition --allow-no-vcs --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` printed `Migrating src\lib.rs from 2021 edition to 2024` and made 3 fixes: `#[no_mangle]` -> `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]` twice and `extern "C" {` -> `unsafe extern "C" {`. It left `edition = "2021"` as it was and left `unsafe { BUF.as_mut_ptr() }` on a static mut as a warning (`creating a mutable reference to mutable static`) for hand work. Then: set edition = "2024", build, run the tests, and run `cargo fix` again without --edition for new warnings. Use --all-features, and one pass per --target that has cfg-gated code.
recipes.rust_version: edition 2024 needs Rust 1.85+; measured on cargo/rustc 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: Code behind inactive features or cfgs is not migrated. The same run also printed `Migrating Cargo.toml from 2021 edition to 2024`, yet the edition key stayed 2021 (measured), so read the manifest, not the log. A rust-version below the edition's first release is a manifest error (measured: `rust-version 1.80 is incompatible with the version (1.85.0) required by the specified edition (2024)`). The edition also picks the default resolver (2021 -> "2", 2024 -> "3"). Raw identifiers (r#gen, r#async) are how a crate on a newer edition calls an item named after a newer keyword.
recipes.engine_note: solver/Cargo.toml is edition 2021 and every export in lib.rs and rapier_law.rs is written `#[no_mangle] pub extern "C" fn`, which 2021 accepts and 2024 rejects (checks below); `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]` already compiles under 2021 on 1.98.1, so the attribute half of a migration can land before the edition changes. The solver's own graph mixes all four editions (rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 is edition 2024 under the 2021 root, measured), so staying on 2021 costs nothing. The full list of what `cargo fix --edition` would change in the solver, and whether it moves the bytes, is the rust-currency lane's.
recipes.verify_note: Ran cargo fix --edition on a solver-shaped cdylib: got 'Migrating src\lib.rs...(3 fixes)' verbatim, exactly the 2 no_mangle+1 extern-C rewrites described, edition key left at 2021, static-mut-ref left as a warning.

recipes.name: Declare rust-version and choose the resolver: edition 2024 makes resolver "3" lock MSRV-compatible versions
recipes.what: rust-version makes Cargo refuse an older toolchain, and resolver "3" (the edition-2024 default, Rust 1.84+) prefers dependency versions whose own rust-version fits when it writes Cargo.lock; resolver "2" (the edition-2021 default) ignores rust-version when it picks versions.
recipes.how: Format: a bare version such as "1.86"; no operators, no pre-release. Measured on cargo 1.98.1: rust-version = "1.99" failed `rustc 1.98.1 is not supported by the following package: msrv@0.1.0 requires rustc 1.99`; `--ignore-rust-version` built it (and `env!("CARGO_PKG_RUST_VERSION")` read 1.99). Locking messages: edition 2021 -> `Locking 1 package to latest compatible version`; edition 2024 with rust-version 1.85 -> `Locking 1 package to latest Rust 1.85 compatible version`; edition 2024 with no rust-version -> `... to latest Rust 1.98.1 compatible version` (the running rustc); edition 2021 plus `[resolver] incompatible-rust-versions = "fallback"` in .cargo/config.toml -> `... to latest Rust 1.80 compatible version` (an opt-in without changing edition). To see the newest versions regardless, `CARGO_RESOLVER_INCOMPATIBLE_RUST_VERSIONS=allow cargo update`.
recipes.rust_version: rust-version respected as of 1.56; resolver "3" requires 1.84+; measured on cargo 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: MSRV-aware resolution acts only when Cargo writes the lockfile; a committed lock is used as it stands. "fallback" prefers compatible versions, it does not forbid others. The resolver is workspace-global: a dependency's resolver setting is ignored and a virtual workspace must set one. rust-version cannot sit below the edition's first release (2024 -> 1.85).
recipes.engine_note: The solver declares no rust-version and is edition 2021, so solver/Cargo.lock was written by resolver 2 without regard to rust-version. The real floor comes from the graph: rapier3d-f64 0.35.3's own Cargo.toml declares edition = "2024" and rust-version = "1.86" (read in the local registry copy), while solver/rust-toolchain.toml pins the compiler that makes the bytes, 1.98.1. Declaring rust-version in solver/Cargo.toml would turn a too-old toolchain into Cargo's clear refusal; whether that touches the digest was not measured.
recipes.verify_note: Reproduced the rust-version rejection message and --ignore-rust-version verbatim, plus 2 of the 3 claimed 'Locking to latest Rust X.Y compatible version' message variants exactly (edition2024 w/o and with rust-version).

recipes.name: Pin the compiler with rust-toolchain.toml and run cargo from that directory: rustup finds it from the cwd
recipes.what: rust-toolchain.toml's [toolchain] table (channel, targets, components, profile) selects the toolchain for commands run in its directory or below, but `cargo +name`, RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN and `rustup override` all outrank it, and it is found from the current directory, not from --manifest-path.
recipes.how: Keys: channel ("stable", "nightly-YYYY-MM-DD", or a version such as "1.98.1"; or `path` for a custom toolchain instead), targets (e.g. ["wasm32-unknown-unknown"]), components (beyond the profile) and profile (minimal = rustc, rust-std, cargo; default adds rust-docs, rustfmt, clippy; a profile only affects newly installed toolchains). Precedence: `+toolchain` > RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN > directory override > rust-toolchain.toml > the default toolchain; the file and directory overrides are found by walking up from the current directory. Measured with rustup 1.29.1 on a scratch copy of solver/: `rustup show active-toolchain` -> `1.98.1-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc (overridden by '<scratch>\solvercopy\rust-toolchain.toml')`; with RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN=stable -> `stable-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc (overridden by environment variable RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN)`. From the parent directory, `cargo build -v --manifest-path solvercopy/Cargo.toml --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown --frozen` ran `...\toolchains\stable-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc\bin\rustc.exe`, and its si_solver line had no `-C target-feature=-relaxed-simd`: neither the toolchain file nor the copy's .cargo/config.toml applied.
recipes.gotchas: A pin that holds only when the cwd is right fails without a sound: stable is also 1.98.1 today, so the wrong toolchain yields the right compiler by coincidence until stable moves. A version channel pins exactly; "stable" floats. An exported RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN (or a `cargo +x` in a script) overrides the file. The minimal profile has no rustfmt or clippy, so jobs that need them must list them in components. What rustup does when the pinned toolchain is not installed is the ci lane's topic.
recipes.engine_note: solver/rust-toolchain.toml (channel "1.98.1", targets ["wasm32-unknown-unknown"], profile "minimal") applies because solver/build.mjs spawns cargo with `cwd: solver`, and that same cwd is what makes solver/.cargo/config.toml apply. `cargo build --manifest-path solver/Cargo.toml` from the repo root gets the default toolchain and no config rustflags (measured on a copy), so builds should go through build.mjs or `cd solver`. A Rust-side clippy or rustfmt job for the solver needs `components = ["rustfmt", "clippy"]` in this file or an explicit install.
recipes.verify_note: Reproduced the central claim precisely: --manifest-path from the parent dir used the default (stable) toolchain and dropped the .cargo/config.toml --cfg flag; running from inside the dir used 1.98.1 and kept it.

recipes.name: Treat Cargo's rustflags sources as exclusive: any RUSTFLAGS, even empty, drops .cargo/config.toml rustflags
recipes.what: Cargo uses only the first of CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS, RUSTFLAGS, all matching [target.<triple>] / [target.<cfg>] rustflags (joined), or [build] rustflags, so exporting RUSTFLAGS to add one flag silently discards a pin kept in .cargo/config.toml.
recipes.how: Measured on cargo 1.98.1 with `[build] rustflags = ["--cfg", "from_build"]` and `[target.x86_64-pc-windows-msvc] rustflags = ["--cfg", "from_target"]`: plain build -> from_target only (a matching target entry silences [build]); RUSTFLAGS="--cfg from_env" -> from_env only; CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS beside RUSTFLAGS -> from_encoded only; RUSTFLAGS="" or CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS="" -> no flags at all. The config-key forms join instead: CARGO_TARGET_X86_64_PC_WINDOWS_MSVC_RUSTFLAGS -> from_target,from_target_env; `--config 'target.x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.rustflags=[...]'` -> from_target,from_cli; CARGO_BUILD_RUSTFLAGS -> from_build,from_env. On a scratch copy of the solver, the config alone put `-C target-feature=-relaxed-simd` on every crate's rustc line; with RUSTFLAGS holding one --remap-path-prefix, the verbose log contained `relaxed-simd` zero times. RUSTFLAGS splits on whitespace: `--remap-path-prefix=C:\A B\.cargo=/cargo` became two arguments and rustc failed `--remap-path-prefix must contain '=' between FROM and TO`, while the same flag in CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS (separator 0x1f) or in a TOML-literal --config array arrived intact. With --target, rustflags reach only target compilations, not build scripts or proc macros.
recipes.gotchas: Exporting RUSTFLAGS for one extra flag removes everything the config held, and a CI step that exports an empty RUSTFLAGS does the same. [build] rustflags stops applying the moment any [target.<triple>] or [target.<cfg>] rustflags entry matches. Flags that profiles manage (opt-level, panic) belong in profiles. wasm32-unknown-unknown's default features track LLVM and have changed (bulk-memory and nontrapping-fptoint became default in 1.87), so an explicit -feature is the durable pin; relaxed-simd is off by default on 1.98.1 (check below).
recipes.engine_note: solver/.cargo/config.toml pins `[target.wasm32-unknown-unknown] rustflags = ["-C", "target-feature=-relaxed-simd"]`, and solver/build.mjs sets RUSTFLAGS for its three --remap-path-prefix flags, which replaces that config; that is why build.mjs repeats `-C target-feature=-relaxed-simd`. Measured on a scratch copy of the real solver source on this rig: dropping the repeat rebuilt to the identical SHA-256 (on 1.98.1 the pin guards a default that could change, it does not move today's bytes), while `+relaxed-simd` produced a different digest; the same flags passed as CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS left all 50 units Fresh (no rebuild, same bytes). Two holes remain in build.mjs: an inherited CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS outranks its RUSTFLAGS and would drop the pin and the remaps, and a cargo-home or checkout path with a space breaks the RUSTFLAGS split. Setting CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS to the flags joined by '\x1f' closes both.
recipes.verify_note: Reproduced the full 4-source exclusivity matrix on 1.98.1: target config silences build config; RUSTFLAGS overrides both; CARGO_ENCODED_RUSTFLAGS wins over RUSTFLAGS; either set to empty yields zero flags, not a fallback.

recipes.name: Delete from a hashed Vec with remove/retain/drain, not swap_remove; pre-size it with with_capacity/reserve
recipes.what: A Vec's order is its index order: remove, retain and drain keep it, swap_remove moves the last element into the hole, and capacity is only a lower bound whose growth the docs leave unspecified.
recipes.how: Pre-size with `Vec::with_capacity(n)` (capacity >= n; the method 'is allowed to allocate for more elements than capacity') or `v.reserve(k)` (capacity >= len + k afterwards). Reuse a per-step buffer with `v.clear()`, which 'has no effect on the allocated capacity'. Remove while keeping order: `v.remove(i)` (shifts the tail, O(n)), `v.retain(|x| keep(x))` (visits each element exactly once in the original order and preserves the order of the retained elements), `v.drain(a..b)` (yields the removed run in order; dropping the Drain unconsumed still removes it). Use `v.swap_remove(i)` (O(1)) only where the order never reaches an output, or sort again before hashing. Never serialise or hash `capacity()`.
recipes.gotchas: `swap_remove(1)` on ['a','b','c','d'] leaves ['a','d','c'] while `remove(1)` leaves ['a','c','d']: same elements, different sequence, different hash. Order-changing removal can also happen inside a dependency: Rapier 0.35.3's graph deletes edges with `edges.swap_remove`, so an iteration order your code never touched still moves. The docs say Vec 'does not guarantee any particular growth strategy when reallocating when full, nor when reserve is called', so `capacity()` after the same pushes is not a portable value. A Drain holds `&mut` on the Vec until it is dropped; leaking it with `mem::forget` may lose elements.
recipes.engine_note: Rapier 0.35.3 removes contact-graph edges with `self.edges.swap_remove(e.index())` (src/data/graph.rs `remove_edge_adjust_indices`), and `NarrowPhase::contact_pairs()` walks that edges vec in index order (`interactions()` -> `raw_edges().iter()`), so pair order changes whenever a contact ends. That is why `rebuild_snapshot` in solver/src/rapier_law.rs collects the pairs into a Vec and sorts them before hashing; it also reuses the snapshot buffer with `out.clear()`, which keeps its capacity.
recipes.verify_note: Raw Vec-docs HTML confirms swap_remove ('does not preserve ordering...O(1)') and retain ('preserves order of retained') verbatim. Both checks pass on rustc 1.98.1; rapier graph.rs's swap_remove edge removal confirmed live.

recipes.name: Let only Vec, VecDeque or BTreeMap/BTreeSet order reach an output; HashMap/HashSet order is random per map
recipes.what: std defines iteration order for sequences (index 0 upward), VecDeque (front to back) and B-trees (key order); HashMap/HashSet iterate in 'arbitrary order' under a randomly seeded hasher that differs per map and per run, and BinaryHeap::iter/into_vec are arbitrary too.
recipes.how: When order can reach bytes, a hash, a log line or a golden, iterate a `Vec`/slice/array (index order), a `VecDeque` (front to back) or a `BTreeMap`/`BTreeSet` (key order; keys must be `Ord`). Keep `HashMap`/`HashSet` to lookups, or collect and sort before emitting: `let mut ks: Vec<_> = m.keys().copied().collect(); ks.sort_unstable();` (map keys are unique, so an unstable sort is safe). Empty a `BinaryHeap` with `pop()` or `into_sorted_vec()` (ascending), never `iter()`/`into_vec()`. Map equality `a == b` ignores order and is safe; `a.iter().eq(b.iter())` compares orders and is not.
recipes.gotchas: Two HashMaps filled by the same inserts in one process iterate differently (measured on 1.98.1), and a second run of the same binary prints yet another order, so a test that compares a run with itself passes. The default hasher is 'currently SipHash 1-3, though this is subject to change at any point in the future': neither std's HashMap order nor its hash values are a persistence contract (fixed-seed hashers, IndexMap and FxHash are covered in float-determinism). `{:?}` of a HashMap follows the same order: the two identical maps printed different Debug text (measured), so never put one in a golden. A BinaryHeap collected from [1, 5, 2, 4, 3] iterates as [5, 4, 2, 1, 3] on 1.98.1: heap array order, not sorted. `BTreeMap<f64, _>` does not compile (E0277, `f64: Ord` is not satisfied).
recipes.engine_note: solver/src (e5fbcb9 and main 4782a8a) holds no HashMap, HashSet or BTreeMap: bodies and colliders live in fixed `static mut` arrays walked in index order, plus `Vec<Option<RigidBodyHandle>>`. Rapier's `contact_pairs()` is Vec-backed but not canonical (see the swap_remove recipe), which is why the snapshot sorts it. Any map added for mesh collision or host bindings should stay off the snapshot path or be a BTreeMap.

recipes.name: Use the map entry API for counters and get-or-insert instead of get_mut followed by insert
recipes.what: `map.entry(k)` searches once and returns an Entry whose `or_insert`, `or_insert_with`, `or_default` and `and_modify` give `&mut V`; the hand-written get_mut / insert / get_mut function that returns the reference is still rejected on 1.98.1 (E0499).
recipes.how: Counter: `*counts.entry(k).or_insert(0) += 1;`. Get-or-create that returns a reference: `fn slot(m: &mut HashMap<u32, Vec<u32>>, k: u32) -> &mut Vec<u32> { m.entry(k).or_default() }`. Update-or-insert: `m.entry(k).and_modify(|hp| *hp -= 5).or_insert(100);`. Costly default: `or_insert_with(|| build())` runs the closure only when the key is vacant. BTreeMap has the same API (`btree_map::Entry`).

recipes.name: Give every hashed sort a unique total key; if keys can tie, use stable sort_by, not sort_unstable_by
recipes.what: `sort`, `sort_by` and `sort_by_key` preserve the initial order of equal elements; `sort_unstable*` 'may reorder equal elements', and since the 1.81 switch to ipnsort its docs no longer carry the pdqsort-era promise of 'a fixed seed to always provide deterministic behavior'. With a unique key, both produce identical output.
recipes.how: Make the comparator a total order with no Equal between distinct elements: `v.sort_unstable_by(|a, b| a.key.cmp(&b.key).then(a.id.cmp(&b.id)))`. With such a key the stable and unstable sorts give the same output, so neither an algorithm change nor a toolchain bump can move it. If ties are possible and the key cannot be extended, use stable `sort_by` / `sort_by_key`: equal elements keep their input order, which must itself be canonical. Guard the invariant in tests: `assert!(v.windows(2).all(|w| cmp(&w[0], &w[1]).is_lt()))`.

recipes.gotchas: Measured on 1.98.1: `sort_unstable_by_key` kept equal keys in input order for 20 elements and reordered them at 21 and 100, so a small unit test hides the difference. Since 1.81 both sorts 'may panic' when the comparator is not a total order, and 'even if the function exits normally, the resulting order of elements in the slice is unspecified'; a cyclic comparator panicked stable `sort_by` on a 50-element input (measured). The 1.82 release notes say the rewritten binary_search 'may select a different value among the equal ones than the old implementation': results that depend on how std treats ties do move between releases.

recipes.name: Sort f64 with sort_by(f64::total_cmp), find first matches with partition_point, and dedup floats by bits
recipes.what: f64 is not Ord, so `sort()`, `sort_by_key(|p| p.x)` and `BTreeMap<f64, _>` fail with E0277; `total_cmp` is IEEE 754 totalOrder (-NaN < -inf < ... < -0.0 < +0.0 < ... < +inf < +NaN); on a sorted slice `binary_search` may return any of several equal matches, and `dedup` removes only consecutive PartialEq-equal runs.
recipes.how: `v.sort_by(f64::total_cmp)`; for records `v.sort_by(|a, b| a.depth.total_cmp(&b.depth).then(a.id.cmp(&b.id)))`. Costly keys (a String, a computed norm): `v.sort_by_cached_key(|b| key(b))` calls the key at most once per element (100 calls for 100 elements against 1406 for `sort_by_key`, measured on 1.98.1). First index of a value in a sorted slice: `s.partition_point(|x| *x < target)`; keep `binary_search` for membership or the insertion point (`Err(i)`). Remove every duplicate: sort, then `dedup()`; for floats compare bits: `v.dedup_by(|a, b| a.to_bits() == b.to_bits())`.
recipes.rust_version: total_cmp 1.62+; sort_by_cached_key 1.34+; partition_point 1.52+; binary_search tie choice changed in 1.82
recipes.gotchas: `a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap()` panics at the first NaN comparison. `unwrap_or(Ordering::Equal)` is not a total order: on 1.98.1 it made `sort_unstable_by` panic on a 100-element input and left a 1000-element `sort_by` output unsorted without any error (both measured). `total_cmp` puts -0.0 before +0.0 while `==` calls them equal, so `dedup()` collapses [-0.0, 0.0] to the first and never merges NaNs. `[1, 2, 2, 2, 3].binary_search(&2)` returns Ok(3) on 1.98.1, not the first match; the docs say the index 'is chosen deterministically, but is subject to change in future versions of Rust', and 1.82 did change it. The order of sort_by_cached_key's key calls 'is unspecified and may change in future versions'.
recipes.engine_note: `rebuild_snapshot` canonicalises -0.0 to +0.0 in `canon()` before `to_le_bytes` (solver/src/rapier_law.rs), and a NaN makes `write_body` / `canon_quat` refuse, so the step returns false. A future sort by an f64 on the snapshot path (contact points by depth, bodies by distance) should compare the canonicalised values with `total_cmp` plus an id tiebreak; on raw values, -0.0 and +0.0 order differently under `total_cmp`, so the same state could sort differently.

recipes.name: Choose iter, iter_mut or into_iter by ownership, and consume every adapter chain you build
recipes.what: `for x in &v` iterates `&T` (iter), `for x in &mut v` iterates `&mut T` (iter_mut), `for x in v` consumes v and yields `T` (into_iter); adapters such as `map` are lazy and run nothing until consumed; from edition 2021, `array.into_iter()` yields values, while 2015/2018 resolve it to `(&array).into_iter()`.
recipes.how: Read-only pass: `for b in &bodies {}`; in-place update: `for b in &mut bodies { b.v *= k; }`; transfer ownership: `for b in bodies {}` or `bodies.into_iter().map(..).collect()`. Run side effects in a `for` loop or `.for_each(..)`, never a bare `.map(..)`. Arrays in a 2021+ crate: `for x in [a, b, c]` and `[a, b, c].into_iter()` both give values; call `.iter()` when you want references.
recipes.rust_version: array into_iter by value: edition 2021+ (IntoIterator for arrays exists in every edition since 1.53)
recipes.gotchas: `v.iter().map(|x| println!("{x}"));` compiles with `unused_must_use` ('iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed') and `map_unit_fn` warnings and prints nothing. After `for s in v`, `v.len()` is E0382 (v was moved by the loop's implicit `.into_iter()`). In an edition-2018 crate `[1, 2, 3].into_iter().collect::<Vec<i32>>()` is E0277 because the items are `&i32`; code that still compiles there gets the `array_into_iter` lint. Only method-call syntax differs by edition; `for e in [1, 2, 3]` iterates by value in every edition.

recipes.what: `zip` ends when either input ends, without error; `windows(k)` yields len-k+1 overlapping slices; `chunks_exact(k)` omits the last len % k elements into `remainder()`; `collect` builds any `FromIterator` target: `Result<Vec<_>, E>` stops at the first Err, and a `BTreeMap` sorts by key and keeps one value per key.
recipes.how: `debug_assert_eq!(pos.len(), vel.len()); for (p, v) in pos.iter().zip(&vel) {}`; `for (i, b) in bodies.iter().enumerate()`; `a.iter().chain(&b)` concatenates in order. Fixed strides: `buf.chunks_exact(STRIDE)` and check `.remainder().is_empty()`, or `let (rows, tail) = buf.as_chunks::<17>();` (1.88+, rows are `&[[f64; 17]]`); neighbour pairs: `windows(2)` or `array_windows::<2>()` (1.94+). Parse or refuse: `let xs: Result<Vec<f64>, _> = toks.iter().map(|t| t.parse::<f64>()).collect();`.
recipes.gotchas: Zipping 4 positions with 3 velocities yields 3 pairs and no error. Over 7 items `chunks(3)` gives lengths [3, 3, 1] while `chunks_exact(3)` gives two chunks and hides [7] in `remainder()`. `windows(0)` and `chunks_exact(0)` panic. Collecting into a HashMap or HashSet brings back arbitrary order; into a BTreeMap, duplicate keys keep one value ('all but one of the corresponding values will be dropped'). `collect::<Result<_, _>>()` stops pulling at the first Err, so side effects in the closure stop there too (measured: '1' and 'x' seen, '3' never parsed).

recipes.name: Sum floats in one canonical order: iter().sum() is a left fold from -0.0 and reordering changes the bits
recipes.what: For f16/f32/f64/f128, `Iterator::sum` is `iter.fold(-0.0, |a, b| a + b)` in iteration order (core at tag 1.98.1); float addition is not associative, so reversing or regrouping the same values changes the result, and an empty float sum is -0.0 since 1.82 (rust-lang/rust#129321).
recipes.how: Sum over a canonical sequence (body index order, or a sorted Vec), never over a HashMap/HashSet or a parallel iterator. Choose the identity on purpose: `.sum::<f64>()` starts at -0.0, `.fold(0.0, |a, &b| a + b)` starts at +0.0; they differ only for empty or all -0.0 input. Canonicalise zero before hashing (`if x == 0.0 { 0.0 } else { x }`, then `to_bits()`). If a total must not depend on order, change the representation (integers, fixed point), not the loop.
recipes.gotchas: [0.1, 0.2, 0.3] sums to 0.6000000000000001 forward and 0.6 reversed; [1e16, 1.0, -1e16] sums to 0.0 while [1e16, -1e16, 1.0] sums to 1.0, and the same holds under -O (measured). The fold docs call order 'not important' for 'associative operators like +'; that is true for integers, not for floats. Before 1.82 the float identity was +0.0, so an empty sum hashed through `to_bits()` changes sign across that release. Parallel reductions (rayon) regroup additions (concurrency-async lane).

recipes.name: Return closures as impl Fn with move, and bound callbacks by the weakest Fn trait the call site needs
recipes.what: A closure captures each variable in the first mode its body allows (shared borrow, unique borrow, mutable borrow, move) and implements FnOnce always, FnMut if it moves nothing out, Fn if it also mutates nothing; `move` forces by-value capture (a copy for Copy types) without changing which Fn traits apply.
recipes.how: Return: `fn scaler(k: f64) -> impl Fn(f64) -> f64 { move |x| x * k }`. Parameters: `F: FnOnce()` when you call it once, `FnMut` when it may mutate captured state (std's `retain`, `sort_by` and `map` take FnMut), `Fn` only when it must be callable through `&`. Store different closures as `Vec<Box<dyn Fn(f64) -> f64>>`. A `move` closure over a Copy value copies it and the original stays usable.
recipes.gotchas: Returning `|x| x * k` without `move` is E0373 ('closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `k`'). Calling a closure that moves a capture out a second time is E0382 ('closure cannot be invoked more than once'). The same mistake, a mutating closure passed to an `F: Fn()` parameter, is reported as E0594 when the closure is written inline (the expected bound drives inference), and a closure that only implements FnOnce, bound to a variable first, is reported as E0525. `move` does not make a closure FnOnce. Edition 2021 captures disjoint fields (ownership-borrowing lane).

recipes.what: String and &str are always valid UTF-8: `len()` counts bytes, `s[i]` does not compile (E0277), `&s[a..b]` panics off a char boundary while `s.get(a..b)` returns None, and Unicode-aware methods follow `char::UNICODE_VERSION`, which the docs say changes over time without that being a breaking change.

Count chars with `s.chars().count()`, walk bytes with `s.bytes()`, find cut points with `s.char_indices()` or `s.is_char_boundary(i)`, slice with `s.get(a..b)`. Decode untrusted bytes with `String::from_utf8(bytes)` (Err on invalid input); `from_utf8_lossy` silently substitutes U+FFFD. For names or ids that reach a hash, compare with `eq_ignore_ascii_case` / `to_ascii_lowercase` or on raw bytes, not with `to_lowercase`. `format!("{:>8.3}", x)`: width 8, and for floats precision is the number of digits after the decimal point.

recipes.name: Give a library one error enum per failure mode and let `?` convert wrapped causes through `From`
recipes.what: `?` on `Err(e)` returns `Err(From::from(e))` from the enclosing function, so an error enum plus one `From` impl per wrapped cause turns each fallible call into a single `?`; since 1.81 the `Error` trait is also in `core::error`, so the same impl serves `#![no_std]` code.
recipes.how: Write `enum LoadError { Parse(ParseIntError), TooManyBodies { n: u32, max: u32 } }`: one variant per condition a caller can act on, carrying the data it needs. Implement `Display` (concise, lowercase, no trailing punctuation), `Error` with `source()` returning the wrapped cause, and `impl From<ParseIntError> for LoadError`; then `s.parse::<u32>()?` converts on its own. A reporter walks the chain: `let mut cur = e.source(); while let Some(c) = cur { ...; cur = c.source(); }`. Where an `Option` meets a `Result` function, name the refusal as you convert: `handles[i].ok_or(Refusal::Carried { body: i })?` (the combinators themselves are the types-patterns lane's). In `#![no_std]` write `impl core::error::Error for T`; the compiler accepts that impl wherever `dyn std::error::Error` is asked for (check 1).
recipes.gotchas: A missing `From` impl is E0277 ("`?` couldn't convert the error to `LoadError`"). `?` never converts between `Option` and `Result`, so a bare `None` carries no reason until `ok_or` names one. Put the wrapped error in `source()` or in the `Display` text, not both, or a chain report prints it twice. Do not use `()` as an error type: it implements neither `Error` nor `Display`, its `Debug` says nothing, and downstream crates cannot write a meaningful `From<()>`. `Error::description` (deprecated 1.42) and `Error::cause` (deprecated 1.33) are dead: implement `Display` and `source()`.

A fieldless `Refusal` enum returned through `?` is the internal type the export recipe in this lane builds on; being `core`-only, it costs nothing on `wasm32-unknown-unknown`.

recipes.name: Derive library error enums with thiserror 2; use anyhow or `Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>` only in binaries
recipes.what: thiserror generates the `Display`, `Error::source` and `From` impls you would write by hand and stays out of your public API; anyhow gives application code one opaque error type with `.context()` layers and a cause-chain printer.
recipes.how: Library: `#[derive(Debug, thiserror::Error)]` with one `#[error("...{n}...")]` per variant (fields interpolate as `{n}`, `{0}`, `{n:?}`); `#[from]` on a variant whose only field is the cause generates `From` and implies `#[source]`; a field named `source` is the source automatically; `#[error(transparent)]` forwards `Display` and `source` to an inner error. Application or tool: return `anyhow::Result<T>`, add `.context("what was being attempted")`, check with `ensure!`, print `{:#}` for `outer: cause` on one line. Without either dependency, `Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync + 'static>` takes any `E: Error + Send + Sync` through `?` and a `&str` or `String` through `.into()`.
recipes.gotchas: A `#[from]` variant may hold no field besides the source (and possibly a backtrace). `anyhow::Error::new` requires `Send + Sync + 'static`; the error is one word wide. `{:?}` on an anyhow error prints a `Caused by:` block and includes a backtrace when one was captured, so never compare it byte for byte in a test. A plain `Box<dyn Error>` is not `Send`: returning it from `thread::spawn` is E0277 ("`dyn std::error::Error` cannot be sent between threads safely"). A library that returns `anyhow::Error` leaves its callers only `downcast_ref` to recover a type; that is where the thiserror/anyhow line falls.

recipes.name: Use `expect` with a 'should' message only for invariants the compiler can't see; return `Result` for input
recipes.what: A panic is for a broken invariant or contract (a bug) and a `Result` for an anticipated failure; `expect("... should ...")` records why a value is guaranteed, while bare `unwrap()` panics with no reason attached.
recipes.how: Default to returning `Result` from anything that can fail on its inputs. Keep `unwrap`/`expect` for tests, prototypes and facts established elsewhere in the code, and phrase the message as a precondition, `.expect("a plan should exist for every kinematic body with a handle")`, the style the std docs recommend over describing the failure. `Result::expect` appends the error's `Debug` (`msg: ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit }`); `Option::unwrap` says only "called `Option::unwrap()` on a `None` value". Document a function's panicking contract in its docs.
recipes.gotchas: In the wasm build an `expect` message reaches no one: `println!` does nothing on `wasm32-unknown-unknown`, the module has no import to print through, and the panic is an abort, so the text serves native runs only. Data that arrives through an export is input: refuse it, never `expect` it. Every `unwrap` left in an export path is a latent trap.

recipes.name: Make refusals impossible to drop silently: `Result` is `#[must_use]`, `Option<()>` and `bool` are not
recipes.what: Discarding a `Result` in an expression statement fires `unused_must_use`, but a refusal returned as `Option<()>`, `bool` or a bare integer compiles with no warning unless the function itself is `#[must_use]`.
recipes.how: Return internal refusals as `Result<(), Refusal>` with an inhabited `Refusal` enum, or put `#[must_use = "a false return is a refusal and must reach the export"]` on each function that reports status through `bool` or `u32`. Promote the lint to an error in CI with `-D unused_must_use`. Discard on purpose with `let _ = f();`, the idiom the Reference names.
recipes.gotchas: The function-based check looks only at an expression statement whose expression is the call: wrapping the call, as in `Some(f())` or `(f(),)`, suppresses it (Reference). `Result<(), E>` with an uninhabited `E` such as `Infallible` is exempt (Reference; check 2). `#[must_use]` on a function in a trait impl does nothing; put it on the trait's declaration.

recipes.name: Know what `panic = "abort"` changes: the hook still runs, then no unwinding, no `Drop`, nothing to catch
recipes.what: Under the abort strategy a panic calls the panic hook and then ends the process: destructors do not run and `catch_unwind`, which catches only unwinding panics, gets nothing; `wasm32-unknown-unknown` compiles with `-C panic=abort` by default and its abort is a trap.
recipes.how: Read a target's strategy with `rustc --print cfg --target <triple>` (1.98.1: `panic="abort"` on `wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `wasm32v1-none`, `panic="unwind"` on the x86_64 Windows host) or `cfg!(panic = "abort")` in code. Use `catch_unwind` only at a boundary that must survive a bug under `unwind`, and wrap captured `&mut` state in `AssertUnwindSafe` knowingly. Report expected failures with `Result`; the std docs say `catch_unwind` is not a general try/catch.
recipes.rust_version: any; `-C panic=immediate-abort` is listed in the rustc book but 1.98.1 rejects it on stable ("requires `-Zunstable-options` and a nightly compiler", measured)
recipes.gotchas: `cargo test` and benches ignore the profile's `panic` setting because the test harness requires unwind, so a `#[should_panic]` test passes natively while the same panic aborts in the release artifact. On this Windows host an abort ends the process through `__fastfail` with status 0xC0000409 (3221226505), not 101. The `catch_unwind` closure must be `UnwindSafe`: capturing `&mut` is E0277 ("may not be safely transferred across an unwind boundary"). Dropping the `Err` payload of `catch_unwind` can itself panic, and catching a foreign exception has unspecified behaviour.
recipes.engine_note: `solver/Cargo.toml` sets `panic = "abort"`, which restates the `wasm32-unknown-unknown` default. In that build std's abort is `core::intrinsics::abort()`, which node reports as `WebAssembly.RuntimeError: unreachable` (measured on a 1.98.1 module; the JS API maps a trap to `RuntimeError`). No `Drop` runs, so a panic partway through `solver_step` can leave `SOLVER` and the `static mut` buffers half-written, and the instance still answers later calls (measured), so the JS side must treat any trap as fatal and re-instantiate (depth: wasm-raw-abi). A native build of the law for a Godot or Unreal host under this profile would end the editor process on any panic.

recipes.name: Under `overflow-checks = false`, `+ - *`, negation, `abs` and shifts wrap; `/ %` and indexing still panic
recipes.what: With overflow checks off (Cargo's release default and the solver's profile) arithmetic overflow wraps in two's complement and an oversized shift amount is masked, but division by zero, `MIN / -1`, `MIN % -1` and out-of-bounds indexing panic in every build.
recipes.how: Know the switches: `-C overflow-checks` defaults to follow `-C debug-assertions`, which is on only at opt-level 0, so plain `rustc` and `cargo test` panic where `-O` and `cargo build --release` wrap. Overflow and panics the compiler can evaluate at build time stop the build even with checks off: `arithmetic_overflow` and `unconditional_panic` are deny-by-default. Guard widths and mask sizes at compile time with `const _: () = assert!(MAX_BODIES <= 64, "...");`.
recipes.gotchas: Treat wrapped overflow as a bug the release build hides: the Reference calls it erroneous, and the test build panics on it. RFC 560's text says shift amounts are "unconditionally masked"; rustc 1.98.1 panics on `1u64 << 64` with checks on (check 3) and returns 1 with them off (check 1), which is what the current Reference's overflow list implies. `-C overflow-checks=off` does not remove bounds checks: indexing is a separate panic (check 4).
recipes.engine_note: `signature()` in rapier_law.rs sets `driven |= 1u64 << i` and `carried |= 1u64 << i` for `i < n_bodies <= MAX_BODIES = 64`, so the largest shift is 63. If MAX_BODIES ever passes 64, the shift by 64 is masked to a shift by 0 under this profile (check 1: `1u64 << 64 == 1`), and body 64 would silently share body 0's bit instead of being refused; `const _: () = assert!(MAX_BODIES <= 64);` next to the constant pins it. Bounds checks stay on regardless: `step()` refuses `n_bodies > MAX_BODIES` before it indexes, so a bad count returns 0 instead of trapping inside `field()`.

recipes.name: Say the overflow intent in the call: `checked_`, `wrapping_`, `saturating_`, `overflowing_`, `strict_` (1.91+)
recipes.what: The method families behave the same under every profile: `checked_*` returns `None`, `wrapping_*` wraps, `saturating_*` clamps, `overflowing_*` returns `(value, overflowed)`, and `strict_*` (stable since 1.91.0) always panics on overflow, whether or not overflow checks are enabled.
recipes.how: Hashes meant to wrap: `h.wrapping_mul(0x100000001b3).wrapping_add(x)`. Sizes that feed a limit: `rows.saturating_mul(cols)` then compare, or `a.checked_mul(b).ok_or(Refusal::TooLarge)?`. Shifts by a run-time amount: `1u64.checked_shl(i)` (`None` at `i >= 64`). An arithmetic invariant that must hold in release: `strict_add`, `strict_mul`, `strict_shl`, `strict_abs`, `strict_neg`. `std::num::Wrapping<T>` makes every operator on a value wrap.
recipes.gotchas: Plain operators in a hash are a profile-dependent bug: the same `h * P + x` panics under the test profile and wraps in release (checks 3-5). `wrapping_shl` reduces the amount modulo the bit width (`rhs % Self::BITS`); it does not shift to zero. A `strict_*` panic is a trap under `panic = "abort"` in wasm, so inside exports prefer `checked_*` feeding a refusal. `strict_div` exists for symmetry: plain `MIN / -1` already panics in release.
recipes.engine_note: `mix_u64` in rapier_law.rs is `h.wrapping_mul(0x100000001b3).wrapping_add(x)`: the hash wraps by design and gives the same bits under `cargo test` (overflow checks on) as in the pinned wasm (off); written with `*` and `+` it would panic natively (check 5). `(rows as usize).saturating_mul(cols as usize)` in `signature()` is the clamp-then-refuse idiom. Native tests of these pure functions therefore see the release arithmetic.

recipes.name: Keep panics out of `extern "C"` exports: refuse through an internal `Result` chain mapped to a `u32` status
recipes.what: Since 1.81 a panic that unwinds out of an `extern "C"` function aborts the process, and `catch_unwind` in the caller cannot stop it; so an export never panics: the code behind it returns `Result<(), Refusal>` through `?`, and one `match` at the boundary produces the status code.
recipes.how: `fn step_inner(..) -> Result<(), Refusal>` with `if n > MAX { return Err(Refusal::TooManyBodies) }` and `canon_quat(..).ok_or(Refusal::BadQuaternion)?`; the export is `#[no_mangle] pub extern "C" fn solver_step(..) -> u32 { match step_inner(..) { Ok(()) => 1, Err(_) => 0 } }` (spelled `#[unsafe(no_mangle)]` in edition 2024). Native tests call `step_inner` and assert which `Refusal` came back. If a native host build must survive a bug, build it with `panic = "unwind"` and wrap each export body in `catch_unwind`; `extern "C-unwind"` is for letting a panic cross on purpose (depth: unsafe-ffi).
recipes.rust_version: 1.81+ (abort on an unwind out of `extern "C"`); `"C-unwind"` since 1.71
recipes.gotchas: With `panic = "unwind"`, whether destructors up to the ABI boundary run before the abort is unspecified; nothing beyond the boundary runs (check 1: the caller's guard never drops). On this Windows host the status is 0xC0000409 and stderr reads "panic in a function that cannot unwind" (measured). A bare 0 carries no reason: keep the `Refusal` inside Rust, and if a host ever needs it, a separate export returning the last refusal code (a suggestion) keeps every existing 1/0 contract intact.
recipes.engine_note: The dispatched cleanup item is already fixed: `rebuild_snapshot` did `continue` on a failed `canon_quat` at `c64f67a`, and `6a33297` changed it to `return false` and made `ensure` check the result; `e5fbcb9` and current `origin/main` keep that. The one `continue` left in `rebuild_snapshot` skips carried bodies (`handles[i]` is `None`), which leave the solver by design. What remains is the shape: `ensure -> signature / build_world / rebuild_snapshot` and `solver_step -> integrate -> write_body` pass `bool`s and `Option`s that a future caller can drop without a warning. A `Result<(), Refusal>` chain with `?` keeps every export's 1/0 ABI unchanged and makes 'refuse, never skip' something the compiler checks.

recipes.name: Treat every by-value use as a move: derive Copy only for plain data, clone on purpose (E0382, E0505, E0204)
recipes.what: Assigning, passing or returning a non-Copy value moves it and kills the source (E0382 on reuse, E0505 if a borrow of it is still live); Copy types are bit-copied implicitly; Clone is an explicit and possibly expensive call.
recipes.how: Read `let b = a;`, `f(a)` and `return a` as moves unless the type is Copy (integers, bool, char, f64, and tuples/arrays whose elements are Copy). A use after a move is E0382 ('borrow of moved value' / 'use of moved value'; inside a loop the label reads 'value moved here, in previous iteration of loop'). Fix E0382 by borrowing (`f(&a)`), by `a.clone()` only when a second owner is really wanted, or by `#[derive(Clone, Copy)]` on small plain-data types; Copy requires Clone and every field Copy, else E0204. Fix E0505 (a move while a reference to the value is still used later) by finishing with the reference first - NLL ends a borrow at its last use - or by passing `&a` instead of `a`.
recipes.gotchas: Copy is always an implicit bitwise copy, so a Copy array or struct of arrays (a whole [f64; 17] row) is duplicated silently on every by-value use. Implementing Copy is part of a type's public API: std says to leave it off if the type may stop being Copy. A type that implements Drop can never be Copy, and `&mut T` is never Copy (copying it would alias). rustc's E0382 help offers `.clone()` 'if the performance cost is acceptable'; check whether a borrow or a reorder is the real fix before paying for a deep copy.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/lib.rs reads every slot as `let ax = *field(bodies, i, 0);`: f64 is Copy, so the value is copied out and the `&mut f64` from `field` dies in that statement. rapier_law.rs copies whole rows the same way (`body_at(i) -> [f64; BODY_STRIDE]`), and `integrate` copies `loaded.controller` out of `&mut Loaded` because `KinematicCharacterController` derives Copy in rapier3d-f64 0.35.3; a non-Copy field on that line would be E0507.

recipes.name: Keep one &mut xor any number of & live at once, and end each borrow at its last use (E0499, E0502, E0506)
recipes.what: A value may have one live mutable reference or any number of live shared ones; since Rust 1.63 NLL is the borrow checker on every edition and a borrow lasts only until its last use, so most conflicts are fixed by reordering rather than by blocks, clones or RefCell.
recipes.how: Read the code as the access that conflicts: E0499 = two live `&mut` (`let a = &mut v; let b = &mut v; a.push(..)`); E0502 = a `&` and a `&mut` overlap (`let first = &v[0]; v.push(x); use(first)`, or `v.push` inside `for x in &v`); E0506 = assigning to a place that is still borrowed; E0503 = reading or writing a place while it is mutably borrowed. Fix: move the last use of the first borrow above the conflicting access; copy the value out (`let first = v[0];` for Copy data) instead of keeping a reference; for iterate-and-mutate, collect the change first and apply it after the loop (`let extra: Vec<_> = v.iter()..collect(); v.extend(extra);`). NLL still rejects returning a borrow on one path while mutating the same data on another (NLL problem case #3, `if let Some(s) = vec.last() { return s; } vec.push(..)` is E0502 on 1.98.1): test without holding the borrow (`if vec.is_empty() { vec.push(..) } vec.last().unwrap()`), or use `map.entry(k).or_default()` for maps.
recipes.rust_version: NLL on every edition since 1.63; problem case #3 still rejected on 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: The four codes are one rule seen through different accesses (second borrow E0499/E0502, assignment E0506, plain use E0503), and all four are fixed by ending the first borrow earlier. The E0506 page still shows a scoped `{ let r = &x; .. }` block as a fix; under NLL a block is unnecessary when the reference is simply not used after the conflict. Polonius Alpha, shown accepting the HashMap `get_mut_or_default` example (RFC 2094's problem case #3 shape), was switched on for nightly only in August 2026 with stabilization aimed before the end of 2026: snippets that compile on nightly can still fail on the pinned 1.98.1.
recipes.engine_note: `step` and `resolve_pair` in solver/src/lib.rs never keep a reference across a write - each read is copied into a local first - so NLL has nothing to reject; keep that order in Phase-2 code. rapier_law.rs `integrate` already uses the collect-then-apply fix: it builds `plans` in one loop and calls `set_next_kinematic_translation` in a second.

recipes.name: Know where two-phase borrows apply: v.push(v.len()) compiles, Vec::push(&mut v, v.len()) is E0502
recipes.what: rustc makes only three implicit mutable borrows two-phase - the autoref of a `&mut self` method call, a mutable reborrow in function arguments, and overloaded compound assignment - and such a borrow acts as a shared borrow until the call activates it; an `&mut` written in source never gets this.
recipes.how: Nest reads inside the call through the receiver: `v.push(v.len())`, `r.push(r.len())`, and `Vec::push(r, r.len())` for an existing `r: &mut Vec<_>` all compile. `Vec::push(&mut v, v.len())` is E0502 because the explicit `&mut v` is an ordinary mutable borrow. The reservation permits reads and shared borrows only, so `v.push(v.pop().unwrap())` is E0499; and indexing activates the borrow at once, so `v[0].push_str(&format!("{}", v.len()))` is E0502 (RFC 2025 names this case). Fix all three by hoisting the argument into a local first: `let n = v.len(); v[0].push_str(&n.to_string());`.
recipes.gotchas: RFC 2025 (2017) scoped two-phase borrows to method-call autoref; today's rustc also applies them to reborrows in function arguments and overloaded compound assignment (rustc-dev-guide), so the RFC text is narrower than current behaviour. Rewriting `v.push(x)` into the fully qualified form with a fresh `&mut v` - by hand, in a macro, or during a refactor - silently loses the two-phase treatment.
recipes.verify_note: rustc-dev-guide confirms the 3-case rule + mem::replace example verbatim but omits indexing. RFC2025(2017) is the sole source for indexing-activates-immediately; I ran that exact example on 1.98.1 myself: still E0502 today.

corrections.claim: RFC 2025 (2017) is the sole warrant for 'indexing activates the borrow immediately' (the v[0].push_str example); rustc-dev-guide (current) covers two-phase borrows generally but omits indexing. Verified via compile_oracle on pinned 1.98.1: still E0502 today.

recipes.name: Pass a held &mut to generic parameters as &mut *r: concrete &mut parameters reborrow, generic T moves (E0382)
recipes.what: A held `r: &mut T` passed where the parameter's type is known to be `&mut T` is implicitly reborrowed (`&mut *r`) and stays usable; passed to a generic `T` or `impl Trait` parameter, the reference itself is moved and the next use is E0382.
recipes.how: Concrete parameters just work: `fn bump(x: &mut f64)`, then `bump(r); bump(r);`. For generic parameters write the reborrow yourself - `consume(&mut *r)`, which is what rustc's help suggests ('consider creating a fresh reborrow of `r` here') - or name the type, `consume::<&mut f64>(r)`. The same split applies to `let`: `let r2 = r;` moves `r`, while `let r2: &mut f64 = r;` (a `let` with an explicit type is a coercion site) reborrows and freezes `r` until `r2`'s last use; re-borrowing `r` inside that window (`bump(r)` while `r2` is still used) is E0499. A mutable reborrow in function arguments is also one of rustc's two-phase borrow sites, so `Vec::push(r, r.len())` compiles.
recipes.rust_version: any; the generic-parameter move is still open upstream on 1.98.1 (rust-lang/rust#108532)
recipes.gotchas: The generic case is a known compiler gap, not a rule you misread: rust-lang/rust#162690 (September 2026) was closed as a duplicate of #108532 ('From::from call doesn't do reborrowing', open since 2023), so `Handle::from(r)` (any `From::from` call) and `fn f(x: impl Sized)` still move a `&mut`. `&mut T` is not Copy (copying it would alias), which is why a moved `&mut` reports E0382 like a moved String. The Reference documents reborrowing thinly - its reborrowing issue (rust-lang/reference#788) is still open - so trust the compiler over prose on edge cases.

A Phase-2 helper written generically (e.g. `fn apply<B: AsMut<[f64]>>(b: B)`) would move `bodies` on the first call and fail with E0382 on the second - pass `&mut *bodies`.

recipes.name: Take &[T], &mut [T] and &str parameters instead of &Vec<T>, &String or &[T; N]
recipes.what: A slice parameter accepts a Vec, an array, any sub-range and a String through deref and unsize coercions; a `&Vec<T>` or `&String` parameter rejects arrays and sub-slices (E0308) and gains nothing unless the callee must grow the collection.
recipes.how: Declare `fn sum(xs: &[f64]) -> f64`, `fn zero(xs: &mut [f64])`, `fn name_len(s: &str) -> usize`; callers pass `&v` (Vec derefs to `[T]`), `&a` (`[T; N]` unsizes to `[T]`), `&v[1..]`, `&mut buf[1..3]`, `&owned_string` and string literals without conversion. Keep `&mut Vec<T>` only when the callee must push or resize: a slice has no `push` (E0599). Clippy's `ptr_arg` (style group, warn) flags `&String`, `&Vec`, `&PathBuf` and `Cow<_>` parameters.

A slice fixes the length for the call: mutate in place, return a new Vec, or take `&mut Vec<T>` when the size must change.

recipes.name: Name lifetimes only where the three elision rules fail: two reference inputs, none, or a struct field (E0106)
recipes.what: Elision gives each elided input its own lifetime, assigns a sole input lifetime to every elided output, and with `&self`/`&mut self` assigns self's lifetime; a returned reference with two candidate inputs and no self, with no reference input, or any reference stored in a struct or enum needs a named lifetime (E0106).
recipes.how: Leave single-input accessors elided: `fn field(bodies: &mut [f64], i: usize, slot: usize) -> &mut f64` means `fn field<'a>(bodies: &'a mut [f64], ..) -> &'a mut f64`. Name one lifetime when the result may come from several inputs: `fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str` (without it E0106 'missing lifetime specifier'). With no reference input (`fn get_str() -> &str`, E0106) return an owned value. In methods the `&self` rule wins silently: `fn pick(&self, fallback: &str) -> &str` that returns `fallback` fails with 'lifetime may not live long enough', which has no error code; name `'a` on both. A struct holding a reference needs a parameter, `struct View<'a> { xs: &'a [f64] }` (a bare `&[f64]` field is E0106); inside `impl<'a> Cursor<'a>` take `&mut self` and return `&'a T`, not `&'a mut self`. Since 1.89 the warn-by-default `mismatched_lifetime_syntaxes` lint flags a lifetime hidden in a return path (`fn iter(&self) -> std::slice::Iter<f64>`); write `Iter<'_, f64>`.
recipes.gotchas: Do not answer E0106 or a lifetime error by adding `'static`: the Book says such suggestions usually mean a dangling reference or mismatched lifetimes. `&'a mut self` on a struct with parameter `'a` keeps the struct mutably borrowed for its whole life, so the second call is E0499; a 2022 ICSE study of 100 Stack Overflow questions shows this exact trap and counts 30 of 118 violations as inter-procedural lifetime mistakes. The 'lifetime may not live long enough' error has no E-code, so the error index cannot explain it.
recipes.engine_note: `field` in solver/src/lib.rs is the rule-2 case: one reference input (`&mut [f64]`) and two `usize`s, so the returned `&mut f64` borrows `bodies` and nothing else. The crate is edition 2021 on 1.98.1, so `mismatched_lifetime_syntaxes` fires on any new helper that returns an `Iter<f64>`-style type beside a reference input.

recipes.name: Keep the owner alive past its last borrow: fix E0597, E0716 and E0515 by binding it or returning owned data
recipes.what: A reference must not outlive what it points to: a named local dropped at the end of its block gives E0597, a temporary dropped at the end of its statement gives E0716, and returning a reference to a local gives E0515; the fix is to bind the owner in the outer scope or to return owned data.
recipes.how: E0597: declare the owner before and outside the scope that uses the reference (`let data = ..;` above the struct or block that borrows it). E0716: bind the temporary to a `let` first (`let s = String::from(..); let r = s.as_str();`), or write `let r = &String::from(..);` - a borrow in the `let` initializer extends the temporary to the end of the block, as do tuple-struct/enum constructor arguments (`let x = Some(&temp());`) and the tail of a block, `if` or `match` in the initializer. Function-call arguments and method receivers are not extended: `let s = String::from("a").as_str();` and `let x = identity(&temp());` are E0716 once `s`/`x` is used. E0515: return the owned value (`Vec<f64>`, `String`, `v.into_iter()`) instead of `&local`. Edition matters: in edition 2021 a temporary in a block's tail expression is dropped after the block's locals, so `let c = RefCell::new(..); c.borrow().len()` as the tail is E0597; edition 2024 drops tail temporaries first and accepts it; in 2021 bind the result to a local and return that.
recipes.rust_version: any; the tail-expression rule differs: edition 2021 E0597, edition 2024 accepted
recipes.gotchas: The E0716 page's own failing example, `let p = bar(&foo());`, is the function-argument case: it looks like the extended `let x = &foo();` but is not. The Reference lists tuple-struct and enum-variant constructor arguments as extending, so `let x = Some(&temp());` compiles on 1.98.1 although it looks like a call. A compiler suggestion to add `'static` is almost never the fix (Book).
recipes.engine_note: solver/ is edition 2021 (solver/Cargo.toml), so a helper whose tail expression creates a guard that borrows a local (the `RefCell::borrow()` shape) hits the 2021 E0597 rule even though the same code compiles in an edition-2024 crate; bind the value to a local before returning.

recipes.name: Move a value out from behind &mut with mem::take, mem::replace or mem::swap instead of fighting E0507
recipes.what: A non-Copy value cannot be moved out of a place behind `&mut` or out of an index (E0507), because the place would be left empty; `std::mem::take`, `std::mem::replace`, `std::mem::swap` and `Option::take`/`replace` move it out while leaving a valid value behind.
recipes.how: `mem::take(&mut self.buf)` returns the old value and leaves `T::default()` (needs `T: Default`). `mem::replace(&mut self.phase, Phase::Done)` returns the old value and installs the one you pass - the state-machine idiom for enums without a Default. `mem::swap(&mut a, &mut b)` exchanges two places. For `Option` fields use `opt.take()` (leaves `None`) and `opt.replace(v)` (leaves `Some(v)`, returns the old option). Moving out by index is the same error (`let s = v[0];` on a `Vec<String>` is E0507): write `mem::take(&mut v[0])` or borrow `&v[0]`.
recipes.rust_version: mem::take 1.40+; mem::replace and mem::swap 1.0+ (const 1.83 / 1.85); Option::take 1.0+, Option::replace 1.31+
recipes.gotchas: rustc's E0507 help offers only 'consider borrowing here' and 'consider cloning the value'; neither hands you ownership without a copy, which is what take/replace do. `mem::take` builds a `Default` value, so use `replace` with an explicit sentinel when Default allocates or has no meaning. `mem::replace` drops neither value: the old one's destructor runs wherever the returned value is dropped.
recipes.engine_note: The solver's `*field(bodies, i, slot)` reads in solver/src/lib.rs work only because the payload is f64 (Copy); the same accessor over a non-Copy payload is E0507. In rapier_law.rs, `Solver { loaded: Option<Loaded>, snapshot: Vec<u8> }` is the state that `ensure` replaces today with `solver.loaded = Some(loaded)`; if T2 `solver_restore` needs the old world or buffer back, `solver.loaded.replace(new)` or `mem::take(&mut solver.snapshot)` returns it by move, with no clone.
