recipes.name: Split one flat buffer into disjoint &mut with split_at_mut, as_chunks_mut and get_disjoint_mut (1.86+)
recipes.what: The borrow checker treats every index of a slice or array as the same place, so `&mut v[i]` and `&mut v[j]` together are E0499 even when i != j; `split_at_mut`, `split_first_mut`, `as_chunks_mut`, `chunks_exact_mut` and `get_disjoint_mut` hand out non-overlapping `&mut` safely.
recipes.how: `let (lo, hi) = v.split_at_mut(mid);` gives `&mut v[..mid]` and `&mut v[mid..]` (panics if `mid > len`; `split_at_mut_checked`, 1.80+, returns `None` instead). `v.get_disjoint_mut([i, j])` (1.86+) returns `Result<[&mut T; 2], GetDisjointMutError>`: `Err(OverlappingIndices)` when the indices overlap, `Err(IndexOutOfBounds)` past the end; indices are all `usize`, all `Range` or all `RangeInclusive`, checked pairwise (O(n^2)). For fixed-stride records, `as_chunks_mut::<STRIDE>()` (1.88+) turns `&mut [f64]` into `(&mut [[f64; STRIDE]], &mut [f64])`, and `get_disjoint_mut([i, j])` on the rows gives two `&mut [f64; STRIDE]`; `chunks_exact_mut(STRIDE)` iterates rows mutably and `slice.swap(i, j)` swaps two elements with no split. rustc's E0499 help for the index case says 'use `.split_at_mut(position)` to obtain two mutable non-overlapping sub-slices'.
recipes.rust_version: split_at_mut 1.0+; split_at_mut_checked 1.80+; get_disjoint_mut 1.86+; as_chunks_mut 1.88+ - all available on the pinned 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: Copying values out first (the resolve_pair shape) is often simpler than splitting and is not a workaround to remove. `get_disjoint_mut` returns `Err` for equal indices, so handle it rather than unwrap when callers can pass i == j. `split_at_mut(j * STRIDE)` needs i < j. `get_disjoint_unchecked_mut` is unsafe: overlapping or out-of-bounds indices are UB even if the references go unused. An array field's elements also borrow as a whole while tuple fields split (`add(&mut p.a[0], &p.a[1])` is E0502, the tuple form compiles); the 2022 ICSE study found this array-vs-tuple difference confused a non-negligible share of participants; split the array with `split_first_mut` or `split_at_mut`.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/lib.rs `resolve_pair(bodies, i, j)` copies every slot it needs into a local through `*field(..)` (7 per body up front, positions re-read before each write), so two `&mut` into the flat `BODIES` buffer (64 bodies x stride 17) never coexist and nothing needs splitting; keep that while the kernel mirrors the JS order. If a rewrite wants both rows mutable at once, use `let (rows, _) = bodies.as_chunks_mut::<BODY_STRIDE>();` then `let Ok([a, b]) = rows.get_disjoint_mut([i, j]) else { return };`, or `bodies.split_at_mut(body_at(j))` with i < j (the only order `step` passes); two `field()` results held together are E0499.

recipes.name: Borrow struct fields directly, not through &mut self getters; edition-2021 closures capture only used fields
recipes.what: Distinct field paths are distinct places, so `&mut w.pos` and `&w.vel` coexist; a `&mut self` getter borrows all of `self`, so two getters held together are E0499; since edition 2021 a closure captures only the field paths it uses.
recipes.how: Borrow fields directly (`let p = &mut w.pos; let v = &w.vel;`) or destructure once: `let World { pos, vel, .. } = &mut w;` gives one `&mut` per field. When the API must be a method, return every borrow the caller needs from one call: `fn parts(&mut self) -> (&mut [f64], &[f64])`. Tuple fields split like struct fields; array elements do not. Closures: in edition 2021 `|x| s.log.push(x)` captures `s.log` only, so `&s.count` may be taken while the closure lives; the same code in edition 2018 captures all of `s` and is E0502. Indexing inside a closure (`|| s.rows[0] += 1.0`) captures the whole `s.rows` field, because RFC 2229 treats all indexing as impure for capture. No stable syntax lets a method declare that it touches only some fields: view types are a 2026 project-goal experiment.
recipes.rust_version: field splitting: any; disjoint closure capture: edition 2021+ (RFC 2229)
recipes.gotchas: Getters such as `fn pos_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Vec<f64>` are the usual source of 'cannot borrow `w` as mutable more than once' in otherwise disjoint code: the borrow checker reads the signature, not the body. Disjoint capture changes when captured values drop and can change whether a closure is Send or Clone; `cargo fix --edition` inserts `let _ = &x;` (lint `rust_2021_incompatible_closure_captures`) to force a whole-variable capture.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs `integrate` already uses the destructuring form: `let PhysicsWorld { broad_phase, narrow_phase, bodies, colliders, .. } = world;` lends four disjoint public fields of one `&mut PhysicsWorld` (rapier3d-f64 0.35.3) to `broad_phase.as_query_pipeline_mut(narrow_phase.query_dispatcher(), bodies, colliders, filter)`. Routing the same call through `&mut self` getters on a wrapper struct would be E0499.

recipes.name: Unit-test the cdylib in #[cfg(test)] modules at the end of each file so the wasm bytes stay put
recipes.what: cargo test --lib builds a cdylib-only crate's #[cfg(test)] modules into a native libtest binary without any crate-type change; the test code never reaches the wasm, but its position can, because line numbers of shipped code are stored in the binary.
recipes.how: Write `#[cfg(test)] mod tests { use super::*; #[test] fn ...() {...} }` as the last item of the file, or `#[cfg(test)] mod tests;` backed by its own file; `use super::*` reaches private functions. Attributes: `#[should_panic(expected = "substring")]` (the test must return `()`), `#[ignore = "reason"]`. Arguments after `--` go to libtest: a positional filter matches any substring of the test path, `--exact` the full path, `--skip F`, `--ignored` / `--include-ignored`, `--list`, `--show-output`, `--test-threads=1`, and `--no-capture` (exposed in 1.88 by rust-lang/rust#139224; `--nocapture` is the deprecated alias and 1.98.1 still accepts it without a warning). Measured on a git-archive copy of solver/ at e5fbcb9, crate-type left at ["cdylib"]: five tests appended to lib.rs and rapier_law.rs; `cargo +1.98.1 test --offline --locked --lib` -> `test result: ok. 5 passed; 0 failed` on x86_64-pc-windows-msvc (19.35 s cold). `cargo +1.98.1 build --offline --locked --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown` then gave SHA-256 c8782b06d03c046ac3b68097bc8e65a55d0fa9e7ae2961d7be038d11d1fdd4e2, byte-identical to the build without tests. Moving the same 23-line module (plus one blank line) to line 2 of rapier_law.rs gave 5be4dd6b54a36f5d...: the 25 differing bytes all sit in the data section and decode as 21 u32 line numbers of rapier_law.rs, each raised by exactly 24 (the other 4 bytes are carries into a second byte). All tests of one binary are threads of one process (alphabetical order when serialised, per the 1.98.1 harness --help): with `--test-threads=1` a test that bumps a static made the next test, which expects a fresh value, fail; each passed alone under `--exact`. cargo-nextest (per its docs; not installed here) runs every test in its own process, which is what running each test alone under `--exact` emulates.
recipes.gotchas: Any edit that changes the line count above a panicking line in solver/src (a test module, a comment) moves the digest; append tests or keep them in their own file. Tests that call step or solver_load share the static mut world with every other test in the binary: parallel threads on static mut are a data race, so serialise and reset, or isolate per process with cargo-nextest. #[should_panic] cannot sit on a Result-returning test, and expected is a substring match. Guides that say --nocapture show the deprecated spelling.

recipes.name: Expect tests/ and doc tests to need an rlib; adding rlib to the solver's crate-type changed its wasm bytes
recipes.what: A cdylib-only crate gives tests/*.rs and doc tests nothing to link: an integration test fails with E0433, plain cargo test skips the doc tests without a word, and cargo test --doc warns then errors. crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"] fixes both, but on a copy of the solver it changed the release wasm's SHA-256.
recipes.how: Measured with cargo 1.98.1 on a two-function crate with crate-type = ["cdylib"]: tests/api.rs calling the crate -> `error[E0433]: cannot find module or crate `cdy` in this scope` (`use of unresolved module or unlinked crate `cdy``). With no tests/ file, `cargo test` printed only the unittests section (no Doc-tests line, no warning, exit 0) although lib.rs carried a /// example. `cargo test --doc` -> `warning: doc tests are not supported for crate type(s) `cdylib` in package `cdy`` then `error: no library targets found in package `cdy``, exit 101. With crate-type = ["cdylib", "rlib"] the unittests, tests\api.rs and Doc-tests sections all ran and passed. Doc tests link only the public API: a /// example calling a private fn failed with `error[E0603]: function `canon` is private`, and the rustdoc book says private items need a unit test. Intra-doc links: write [`mix_f64`] in a doc comment; an unresolved one gives `warning: unresolved link to `canon_quat`` under rustdoc::broken_intra_doc_links (warn by default, cargo doc still exits 0, and cargo doc works on a cdylib-only crate); `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc` makes it an error (exit 101). Re-pin evidence on a git-archive copy of solver/ at e5fbcb9, `cargo +1.98.1 build --offline --locked --release --target wasm32-unknown-unknown`: ["cdylib"] -> c8782b06d03c046ac3b68097bc8e65a55d0fa9e7ae2961d7be038d11d1fdd4e2 (1,526,380 bytes, reproduced on rebuild); ["cdylib", "rlib"] -> 8191738eccd8cffbfadfef5f56879a4bcc4cd1997f251f7fd3ddb974ccbd54d7 (1,526,408 bytes). The type, function, code (+28 bytes) and name sections differ; Cargo passed -C metadata=648e556cfabde42d versus abbc9578777e9c76, the second in one rustc call with both --crate-type flags. A two-function toy crate kept identical bytes either way (eeef8150...), so measure rather than assume.
recipes.gotchas: The 2019 report (rust-lang/cargo#6659, still open) shows E0463 for extern crate; 1.98.1 with 2021-edition paths reports E0433, so search for both. A silently skipped doc test is a harness that cannot fail. Doc tests of private functions cannot compile at all, so for the solver an rlib buys only tests of its extern "C" exports. The byte change was measured on Windows builds and its mechanism was not isolated beyond the -C metadata difference. cargo-nextest does not run doc tests; run cargo test --doc as its own step.
recipes.engine_note: solver/Cargo.toml has crate-type = ["cdylib"]: keep it unless a tests/ harness is worth re-pinning fixtures/solver.sha256. The helpers worth testing are private, so unit tests in the same files are the reachable form, and any /// example added to solver/src is never run by cargo test today.

recipes.name: Run cargo test and cargo test --release: the release run wraps integer overflow that the debug run panics on
recipes.what: cargo test uses the test profile (inherits dev, overflow checks on); --release is --profile=release, so a crate whose release profile sets overflow-checks = false runs its tests with wrapping arithmetic, the shipped behaviour. panic = "abort" is ignored for test builds, and rustc itself refuses --test with -C panic=abort.
recipes.how: Measured with cargo 1.98.1 on a crate whose [profile.release] copies the solver's (opt-level 3, lto false, codegen-units 1, panic abort, overflow-checks false): `cargo test` -> `Finished `test` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo]`, both #[should_panic] tests pass; `cargo test --release` -> `Finished `release` profile [optimized]`, the test expecting `u32::MAX * 17` to panic fails with `note: test did not panic as expected`, while the explicit-panic test still passes although the profile says panic = "abort". rustc 1.98.1 rejects `--test -C panic=abort`: `building tests with panic=abort is not supported without `-Zpanic_abort_tests``. rustc's own default ties overflow checks to debug-assertions, which are on only at opt-level 0, so `-O` alone turns them off (check). Write arithmetic that must not depend on the profile explicitly (`wrapping_mul`, `checked_add`).
recipes.gotchas: A green cargo test does not describe the wasm: the artifact wraps where the debug test panicked. The Cargo book notes that with the abort strategy a test build also forces its dependencies to unwind; abort-mode tests need the unstable panic-abort-tests flag. cargo test --release rebuilds the dependency tree optimised, which is slower.

recipes.name: Rely on rustc for constant overflow and NaN ==, and on Clippy's pedantic float_cmp and cast lints for the rest
recipes.what: rustc denies overflow it can evaluate at compile time (arithmetic_overflow, overflowing_literals, unconditional_panic) and warns on == f64::NAN; it accepts `1088 as u8` and `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` without a word, even under #![deny(clippy::...)]. Clippy's float_cmp and cast_possible_truncation are the lints written for those, and they run only under cargo clippy.
recipes.how: Measured on 1.98.1: `let bytes: u8 = 255 + 1;` -> `error: this arithmetic operation will overflow`; `let lit: u8 = 1088;` -> `error: literal out of range for `u8``; indexing a [f64; 1088] at 1088 -> `error: this operation will panic at runtime`; `y == f64::NAN` -> `warning: incorrect NaN comparison`; `(MAX_BODIES * BODY_STRIDE) as u8` prints 64 and `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` prints false with no diagnostic. The Reference: tool lints are only checked when the tool is active. Clippy as shipped at tag 1.98.1 (src/tools/clippy/clippy_lints): float_cmp is pedantic and exempts comparisons with zero and functions named *eq*; float_cmp_const is restriction; cast_possible_truncation, cast_sign_loss and cast_precision_loss are pedantic; undocumented_unsafe_blocks is restriction (since 1.58.0) and wants a `// SAFETY:` comment on the line(s) directly above the block. Groups: correctness deny; suspicious, style, complexity, perf warn; pedantic, restriction, nursery, cargo allow, so these lints stay off until named. Enable them one by one (`[lints.clippy] float_cmp = "warn"`) rather than the restriction group, which Clippy's README says should not be enabled as a whole. Install with `rustup component add clippy`; fail on warnings with `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`, or with `CARGO_BUILD_WARNINGS=deny cargo clippy`, which Clippy's README prefers because it does not invalidate build caches.
recipes.gotchas: The compile-time lints see only values the compiler can evaluate: the same overflow behind std::hint::black_box compiles and then panics or wraps by profile. float_cmp exempts comparisons with zero, so the solver's `x == 0.0` signed-zero test is never flagged; a bit-level (to_bits) test has to guard it. Read a lint's group from its declaration at the pinned tag; the JS-rendered lint list is easy to misread.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/lib.rs sizes its buffers from MAX_BODIES = 64 and BODY_STRIDE = 17 (1088 slots): rustc stops a literal or constant expression that overflows, but not an `as` cast that truncates. canon's `if x == 0.0` sits inside float_cmp's zero exemption, so float_cmp says nothing about the rule that makes -0.0 hash like 0.0.
recipes.verify_note: Oracle 3/3 pass incl. no_warnings gate. Clippy source at 1.98.1 confirms FLOAT_CMP=pedantic/FLOAT_CMP_CONST=restriction/CAST_*=pedantic; float_cmp.rs's is_allowed() proves the zero/inf exemption covers canon's own x==0.0. Consts confirmed.

recipes.name: Give lint groups priority = -1 in Cargo's [lints] table; add clippy and rustfmt to the pinned toolchain file
recipes.what: Cargo turns [lints] into --allow/--warn/--deny flags ordered by priority, not by position in the file; at equal priority a group can come last and override a member lint (measured), which clippy::lint_groups_priority flags. The pinned 1.98.1 minimal toolchain has neither cargo clippy nor cargo fmt.
recipes.how: [lints] is respected from Cargo 1.74 (announced 2023-11-16): `[lints.clippy] pedantic = { level = "warn", priority = -1 }`, then single-lint overrides at the default priority 0. Measured with `cargo +1.98.1 build -v`: `unused = "deny"` and `unused_variables = "allow"` at equal priority passed `--allow=unused_variables --deny=unused` in either file order and failed with `error: unused variable: `scratch`` and `-D unused-variables implied by -D unused`; with `unused = { level = "deny", priority = -1 }` Cargo passed `--deny=unused --allow=unused_variables` and the build succeeded. On rustc's command line the later flag wins (checks). Clippy's lint_groups_priority (correctness, since 1.78.0): the file order is ignored and without priority the sort order is undefined. Toolchain: add `components = ["clippy", "rustfmt"]` to rust-toolchain.toml (rustup installs listed components on top of the profile; minimal is rustc, rust-std, cargo). Measured: `cargo +1.98.1 fmt --check` -> `error: 'cargo-fmt.exe' is not installed for the toolchain '1.98.1-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc'` (exit 1), `cargo +1.98.1 clippy` -> the same for cargo-clippy.exe; rustup 1.29.1 lists clippy, rustfmt, rust-analyzer and llvm-tools as available for 1.98.1. `cargo fmt --check` exits 0 when rustfmt would change nothing and 1 when it would; config lives in rustfmt.toml or .rustfmt.toml. Warnings gate: build.warnings / CARGO_BUILD_WARNINGS (respected as of Cargo 1.97; warn, allow, deny; local packages only). Measured: `CARGO_BUILD_WARNINGS=deny cargo +1.98.1 build` on a crate with one unused variable -> `error: warnings are denied by `build.warnings` configuration`, exit 101, and the next plain build finished without recompiling. rust-analyzer: `rust-analyzer.check.command` defaults to "check" (set "clippy"); `rust-analyzer.cargo.target` defaults to null, no override (set "wasm32-unknown-unknown" to analyse the artifact's cfgs); `rust-analyzer.cargo.cfgs` defaults to ["debug_assertions", "miri"].
recipes.gotchas: [lints] applies to the current package only, never to dependencies. A -D warnings gate on the solver fails on day one: a copy at e5fbcb9 emits 7 static_mut_refs warnings under 1.98.1 (edition 2021, where the lint is warn-by-default as part of rust_2024_compatibility). Because rust-analyzer turns cfg(miri) on by default, code under cfg(not(miri)) shows as inactive in the editor.
recipes.engine_note: solver/rust-toolchain.toml pins channel 1.98.1, profile minimal and target wasm32-unknown-unknown with no components, and solver/Cargo.toml has no [lints] table; a lint gate needs both. The 7 static_mut_refs sites (lib.rs lines 28, 33, 183, 184; rapier_law.rs lines 78, 738, 743) belong to the unsafe-ffi rewrite.

recipes.name: Suppress lints with #[expect(lint, reason = "...")] (1.81+) instead of #[allow], so a stale suppression warns
recipes.what: #[expect] silences a lint and emits unfulfilled_lint_expectations once the lint stops firing, while #[allow] goes stale silently. rustc never checks an #[expect(clippy::...)] (only a Clippy run does), and an expectation that holds on the host can be unfulfilled on wasm32.
recipes.how: Stable since 1.81 (announced 2024-09-05). Measured on 1.98.1: `#[expect(unused_variables, reason = "...")]` over an unused binding compiles silently; once the binding is used, rustc prints `warning: this lint expectation is unfulfilled`, the reason as a note, and `#[warn(unfulfilled_lint_expectations)]` on by default; under -D warnings that is an error. `#[expect(clippy::float_cmp)]` on code without a float == stays silent under rustc. The Reference: an expectation is fulfilled only by emissions it suppressed itself, an inner allow or warn leaves it unfulfilled, and for a lint group one emitted member suffices. Scope target-dependent expectations with cfg_attr: `#[cfg_attr(not(target_arch = "wasm32"), expect(unused_variables, reason = "..."))]`.
recipes.gotchas: The reason text is printed in the diagnostic, so write it for the reader. The 1.81 announcement's own example, #[expect(clippy::undocumented_unsafe_blocks)] during a migration, is only ever checked by cargo clippy. A plain #[allow] never reports that it has become unnecessary.
recipes.engine_note: Once native tests exist, solver/src compiles for two targets (the host for cargo test, wasm32-unknown-unknown for the artifact); an #[expect] tied to cfg(target_arch) code holds on one and warns on the other (checks), so scope it with cfg_attr.

recipes.name: Property-test the solver's float helpers with proptest over prop::num::f64::ANY, not only hand-picked values
recipes.what: A proptest over f64::ANY on a verbatim copy of canon_quat failed in 6 of 6 runs: an infinite component returns Some((NaN, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)), and a finite one whose square overflows (sqrt(f64::MAX) = 1.3407807929942596e154; measured at 1.4e154 and 1e200) returns Some((0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)), though its doc comment says unit quaternion. proptest shrinks each failure and replays saved seeds.
recipes.how: `proptest! { #[test] fn name(x in prop::num::f64::ANY, ...) { prop_assert!(...) } }` with proptest 1.11.0. f64::ANY includes infinities and quiet NaNs, not signalling NaNs; ranges such as `0u32..1000` shrink toward their start and never leave the range. Measured: `n in 0u32..1000` against `n <= 64` -> `minimal failing input: n = 65` on three runs; in a crate layout the failure was saved to proptest-regressions/lib.txt as `cc <64 hex digits> # shrinks to n = 65` under a header recommending source control. Commit that directory: saved cases replay before novel ones. Config: cases 256 (PROPTEST_CASES); failure_persistence FileFailurePersistence::SourceParallel("proptest-regressions"); rng_seed random unless RngSeed::Fixed(u64) or PROPTEST_RNG_SEED. The six canon_quat runs shrank to x = -1.1869936194728579e203; x = -inf; z = inf; z = -inf; y = -2.309088135335261e260; z = -inf: the seed differs per run, the defect does not. With `rng_seed: RngSeed::Fixed(20260925)` the shrink landed on `x = 0.0, y = 0.0, z = -inf, w = 0.0` (n2 = NaN) in all three oracle runs. A wasm32-unknown-unknown build of the same code returns the same edge values (checks).
recipes.gotchas: With a random seed a rare failure can pass locally and fail in CI; commit proptest-regressions/ or fix the seed. A test file compiled outside a crate layout prints `FileFailurePersistence::SourceParallel set, but failed to find lib.rs or main.rs` and saves nothing. A property must state the contract: js_min(1.0, NaN) returns 1 while node 22's Math.min(1, NaN) returns NaN, so a property against Math.min either excludes NaN or reports that asymmetry.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src/rapier_law.rs canon_quat (used by quat_from_body): once the sum of squares overflows (a single component beyond about 1.34e154, less when several are large) it returns Some((0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)), which quat_from_body hands to Rotation::from_xyzw, and plus or minus infinity yields a NaN component instead of None. T3's planned refusal of non-finite literals would stop infinity but not 1e200; refusing out-of-range values at load or rescaling before squaring is an engine decision.

recipes.name: Prove each Rust harness can go red: cargo-mutants on unit tests, insta goldens that CI cannot auto-accept
recipes.what: cargo-mutants copies the tree, runs cargo test per mutant, replaces an f64 body with 0.0, 1.0 or -1.0 and swaps == with !=; a mutant no test kills is 'missed' (exit 2). For the solver's canon, assert_eq!(canon(-0.0), 0.0) misses the ==-to-!= mutant because -0.0 == 0.0, and a to_bits assertion catches it. An insta golden fails on a mismatch by default; cargo insta test and INSTA_FORCE_PASS=1 force it to pass.
recipes.how: `cargo install --locked cargo-mutants`, then `cargo mutants` in the crate: it copies the tree to a scratch directory (without .git and target), requires a green baseline `cargo test` (exit 4 otherwise), marks a mutant unviable when `cargo test --no-run` fails, and writes mutants.out/ (caught.txt, missed.txt, timeout.txt, unviable.txt, outcomes.json; the previous run becomes mutants.out.old). Exit codes: 0 all caught, 2 missed, 3 timeouts, 4 baseline failing. Mutations include float bodies -> 0.0 / 1.0 / -1.0, == <-> !=, < and > -> == and each other, + <-> - and *, and deleting unary - and !. Hand-applied in the checks: the ==-to-!= mutant of canon passes the == test and fails the to_bits test; the body-to-0.0 mutant passes the -0.0 bit test and fails canon(1.5); each assertion kills different mutants. insta 1.48.0: assert_snapshot! / assert_debug_snapshot! store snapshots/*.snap next to the test; INSTA_UPDATE=auto behaves as no in CI and as new (.snap.new files pending review) elsewhere; always, unseen and force write snapshots; `cargo insta review` accepts or rejects; `cargo insta test` forces snapshot assertions to pass so they are collected (--no-force-pass turns that off); INSTA_FORCE_PASS=1 forces a pass.
recipes.gotchas: A missed mutant can be equivalent to the original ('undistinguishable from the correct code'). cargo-mutants runs cargo test, so in a cdylib-only crate doc tests never count. A golden gate that runs cargo insta test or sets INSTA_FORCE_PASS=1 cannot fail, and INSTA_UPDATE=always rewrites the .snap files unasked; the CI step is plain cargo test, where auto means no. cargo-mutants and cargo-insta are not installed on this rig (`no such command`): their behaviour here is from their documentation, and the checks apply the mutants by hand.
recipes.engine_note: PHASE-2 requires each harness to be shown red; for solver/ that is cargo mutants reporting no missed mutants on the native tests. canon, js_min, js_max and canon_quat encode signed-zero rules that == cannot see, so their tests assert on to_bits.

recipes.name: Add what rustc cannot check: Miri on native tests (nightly only), cargo-deny and cargo-audit on dependencies
recipes.what: Miri interprets cargo miri test and reports out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, uninitialised reads, misalignment, invalid values and data races, but it is a nightly component (1.98.1 offers none) with no FFI; cargo-deny lints the dependency graph (advisories, bans, licenses, sources) from deny.toml, and cargo-audit checks dependencies against the RustSec Advisory Database.
recipes.how: Miri: `rustup +nightly component add miri`, then `cargo +nightly miri test`; on Windows add `--target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` for better system-API support; mark tests Miri cannot or should not run with `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore)]` (it is an interpreter, slower than compiled code); `--target` also cross-interprets other architectures. Measured: `rustup component list --toolchain 1.98.1` offers clippy, rustfmt, rust-analyzer and llvm-tools but no miri, and `cargo +1.98.1 miri` answers `the 'miri' component which provides the command 'cargo-miri.exe' is not available for the '1.98.1-x86_64-pc-windows-msvc' toolchain`; under Cargo's check-cfg, cfg(miri) raises nothing while a typo (mirii) warns `unexpected `cfg` condition name: `mirii`` with `there is a config with a similar name: `miri``. cargo-deny: `cargo install --locked cargo-deny && cargo deny init && cargo deny check`; advisories covers vulnerable, unmaintained and yanked crates, bans covers named crates and duplicate versions. cargo-audit: `cargo install cargo-audit`, then `cargo audit` at the top of the project; `--ignore` or audit.toml waives an advisory; `cargo audit bin` audits built binaries.

recipes.name: Define traits with required and default methods; state generic bounds inline or in a where clause
recipes.what: A trait's body-less methods are required and its methods with bodies are defaults an implementor may override; generic code can call only what its bounds name.
recipes.how: Write `trait Solid { fn half_extents(&self) -> [f64; 3]; fn volume(&self) -> f64 { let [x, y, z] = self.half_extents(); 8.0 * x * y * z } }`. Every `impl Solid for T` must supply each required item (a missing one is E0046) and may override `volume`. Bound generic code inline (`fn total<T: Solid>(..)`) or, once the list grows, with `where T: Solid + Debug`; the Reference defines the two spellings as the same bound. Inside the body only methods of the named bounds resolve: `.volume()` on an unbounded `T` is E0599 ('items from traits can only be used if the type parameter is bounded by the trait'), and a caller whose type lacks the impl gets E0277 ('the trait bound `f64: Solid` is not satisfied').
recipes.gotchas: An overriding method cannot call the default it replaces (the Book says so), so put shared logic in a separately named helper that both call. Overriding a default does not excuse a missing required item (the E0046 check below overrides `volume` and still fails). Adding a body-less method to a published trait breaks every existing impl with E0046; adding one with a default body does not trigger E0046.
recipes.engine_note: solver/src (lib.rs, rapier_law.rs) declares no trait, impl block or derive today (read at origin/main 4782a8a; solver/ is unchanged since 2c2631f): the law is free functions over static f64 buffers. A trait earns a place only where two implementations must be interchangeable; whether the box law and the product law share one is traits-advanced's hook.

recipes.name: Prefer monomorphized generics; use Box<dyn Trait> for mixed-type collections or to cut code size
recipes.what: Generic code is compiled once per concrete type (static dispatch, inlinable, no run-time dispatch cost, paid for in compile time and binary size); a dyn Trait call goes through a vtable (one copy of the code, a run-time lookup, no inlining) and is what lets one container hold different types.
recipes.how: Default to `fn total<T: Solid>(items: &[T])`: calls resolve at compile time and can be inlined. When one Vec must hold `Cube` and `Slab` together, store `Vec<Box<dyn Solid>>` (or pass `&dyn Solid`); each call then finds the method through the vtable at run time. A pointer to a trait object is a data pointer plus a vtable pointer: `size_of::<&dyn Solid>()` is two `usize`, `size_of::<&Cube>()` is one. Write `dyn` explicitly: from edition 2021 a bare `Box<Solid>` is error E0782.
recipes.gotchas: `total(&[Cube(0.5), Slab(..)])` with a generic `T` is E0308: a type parameter is one concrete type per instantiation, which is the moment people reach for dyn. Monomorphization is not free: rustc's own guide names compile time and binary size as the price, and Effective Rust (2024) suggests trait objects when code size or compile time matters. Not every trait can be used as dyn (dyn compatibility, traits-advanced). In editions 2015/2018 a missing `dyn` is only the `bare_trait_objects` warning, so old code breaks at the edition bump, not before.
recipes.engine_note: The solver's bodies are rows of one flat f64 buffer (`BODIES`, stride 17 in solver/src/lib.rs) and a body's kind is a slot value, so no call site in solver/src needs dyn today; if heterogeneous shapes or laws appear, a generic or an enum plus match (types-patterns) keeps dispatch static.

recipes.what: `impl Trait` in argument position is an anonymous generic parameter; in return position the function picks one concrete type the caller cannot name, and every return path must produce that same type.
recipes.how: `fn sum_two(a: &impl Solid, b: &impl Solid)` takes two independently chosen types (with `<T: Solid>(a: &T, b: &T)` both must be the same, E0308 otherwise). `fn ticks(n: u32) -> impl Iterator<Item = f64> { (0..n).map(|i| i as f64 / 64.0) }` returns an unnameable closure adapter with no box and no dynamic dispatch. When branches produce different types, return `Box<dyn Solid>` (a heap allocation plus vtable calls) or an enum.

recipes.gotchas: Returning `Slab` from one branch and `Cube` from the other under `-> impl Solid` is E0308 ('`if` and `else` have incompatible types'). Callers cannot turbofish an impl-Trait parameter: `show::<Cube>(..)` is E0107 with the note '`impl Trait` cannot be explicitly specified as a generic argument'; use a named `<T: Solid>` when callers must choose. For the same reason, switching a public parameter between `impl Trait` and `<T: Trait>` changes the number of generic arguments and can break callers (the Reference says so). impl Trait is allowed only in function argument and return types: `let c: impl Solid = ..` is E0562. recipes.name: Derive Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq and Default on plain data; implement Display by hand
recipes.what: A derive is legal only when every field implements the trait, and each carries a contract: Copy is an implicit bitwise copy that requires Clone, derived Default uses each field's default, derived Debug output is not stable across Rust versions, and Display cannot be derived.
recipes.how: `#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Default)] struct Vec3 { x: f64, y: f64, z: f64 }` gives `{:?}` output, implicit copies, field-wise ==, and `Vec3 { x: 1.0, ..Default::default() }`. For an enum put `#[default]` on a unit variant (1.62+). Write Display yourself: `impl fmt::Display for Vec3 { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result { write!(f, "({}, {}, {})", self.x, self.y, self.z) } }`, which also provides `to_string()`. A hand-written Clone on a Copy type must be equivalent to `*self`.
recipes.gotchas: `#[derive(Clone, Copy)]` on a struct with a Vec field is E0204. There is no Display derive ('cannot find derive macro `Display` in this scope'), and `#[default]` on a variant with fields is rejected ('may only be used on unit enum variants'). Derived Debug formats may change with future Rust versions: never hash, golden-test or parse `{:?}` output. Copy is part of the public API, and a type that implements Drop can never be Copy. On a generic struct a derive adds `T: Trait` bounds to the generated impl.
recipes.engine_note: Snapshot bytes in solver/src/rapier_law.rs are written value by value with `push_f64` (`canon(x).to_le_bytes()`), never through Debug formatting. Keep it that way: derived Debug output may change across Rust versions, which would move a golden on a toolchain bump (the toolchain is pinned to 1.98.1 by solver/rust-toolchain.toml).

recipes.name: Derive only PartialEq and PartialOrd on structs with f64 fields; derived Eq, Hash and Ord fail with E0277
recipes.what: f64 implements PartialEq and PartialOrd but not Eq, Ord or Hash, so derives stop at the partial traits, and the derived == inherits float semantics: NaN is unequal to itself and 0.0 equals -0.0.
recipes.how: For a struct with an f64 field, `#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, PartialOrd)]` is as far as derive goes. `derive(Eq)`, `derive(Hash)` and `derive(Ord)` each fail with E0277 ('the trait bound `f64: Eq` / `f64: Hash` / `f64: Ord` is not satisfied'). With the derived impls a value holding NaN is not equal to itself, `partial_cmp` returns None, and values at +0.0 and -0.0 compare equal though their bits differ. When you need an Eq/Hash/Ord key, wrap the float and build all the impls from its bits (next recipe).
recipes.gotchas: The common wrong fix is `impl Eq for Pose {}`: it compiles (Eq has no methods, so the compiler cannot check reflexivity) and is a logic error once a NaN arrives. A HashSet then holds two 'NaN' entries and cannot find either. std calls this a logic error: behaviour unspecified, not UB, and unsafe code must not rely on these impls. Derived PartialOrd compares fields in declaration order, so reordering fields changes the ordering. assert_eq! on a struct holding NaN fails even when compared with itself.
recipes.engine_note: For T2 (`solver_restore`: restore, rerun, require an identical trace), compare restored state with `to_bits()`, not with a derived `==`: derived PartialEq calls 0.0 and -0.0 equal and NaN unequal to itself, while the hashed snapshot compares bits. The law also uses float == on purpose: `canon` in rapier_law.rs (`if x == 0.0 { 0.0 } else { x }`) folds -0.0 into +0.0 because -0.0 == 0.0, and in `signature` each value passes `bad` (`x.is_nan()`) before it is mixed into `geom`.

recipes.name: Key f64 values by their bits: Eq and Hash from to_bits, Ord from total_cmp, never partial_cmp().unwrap()
recipes.what: `f64::total_cmp` (1.62) orders every bit pattern by IEEE 754 totalOrder and `to_bits` (1.20) exposes the exact pattern; total_cmp compares a sign-adjusted copy of the bits as i64, so it reports Equal exactly when the bits match, and Eq/Hash from to_bits plus Ord from total_cmp form one consistent key.
recipes.how: `#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)] struct Bits(f64);` with `impl PartialEq for Bits { fn eq(&self, o: &Self) -> bool { self.0.to_bits() == o.0.to_bits() } }`, `impl Eq for Bits {}`, `impl Hash for Bits { fn hash<H: Hasher>(&self, h: &mut H) { self.0.to_bits().hash(h) } }`, `impl Ord for Bits { fn cmp(&self, o: &Self) -> Ordering { self.0.total_cmp(&o.0) } }`, `impl PartialOrd for Bits { fn partial_cmp(&self, o: &Self) -> Option<Ordering> { Some(self.cmp(o)) } }`. Sort plain slices with `v.sort_by(f64::total_cmp)`, giving [-NaN, -inf, -0.0, 0.0, 1.5, inf, NaN]. If numerically equal values must collide, canonicalise before keying (map -0.0 to 0.0, refuse NaN). A struct whose float fields are stored as `to_bits()` u64 can simply derive PartialEq, Eq and Hash.
recipes.gotchas: `sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap())` panics as soon as it meets a NaN (exit 101). total_cmp disagrees with ==: -0.0 sorts before +0.0, and NaNs of different sign or payload are different keys (a negative NaN sorts first, and Debug prints both as `NaN`). Mixing policies breaks the Hash/Eq rule (k1 == k2 implies hash(k1) == hash(k2)): a derived PartialEq (0.0 == -0.0) paired with a to_bits Hash hashes equal keys differently. `ordered_float::OrderedFloat` 5.5.0 picks the opposite policy (±0 equal; NaN equal to itself and greater than everything). Choose one policy per key type and build all four impls from it. std says data fed to a Hasher by Hash is not portable across platforms or stable across compiler versions, so a persisted or golden hash should hash explicit bytes (`to_le_bytes`, `to_bits`) with a hasher that documents stability (sim-architecture lane), never a derived Hash through std's hashers.
recipes.engine_note: `mix_f64(h, x)` in solver/src/rapier_law.rs is `mix_u64(h, x.to_bits())` (multiply by 0x100000001b3, add; seed 0xcbf29ce484222325), so 0.0 and -0.0 feed different words. `push_f64` writes `canon(x).to_le_bytes()` into the snapshot, but `signature` mixes raw collider and height values into `geom`, and `same_sig` compares `geom`: a collider coordinate of -0.0 therefore signs a different world (reload) than 0.0. That is a reading of the code, not a measured failure, and worth one test. `Signature` already keys its float by bits (`cell: u64` = `cell.to_bits()`), so every field is an integer and `#[derive(PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]` would be legal and would replace the hand-written `same_sig`, which silently ignores a field someone forgets to add. The snapshot pair sort keys on pairs of `(u32, u32)` tuples from `into_raw_parts()`; ColliderHandle itself derives Eq and Hash but not Ord in rapier3d-f64 0.35.3, so it cannot be sorted directly, and integer tuples need no float comparator.

recipes.what: From is for infallible, lossless conversions and gives Into for free through a blanket impl, so a hand-written Into for the same pair collides (E0119); TryFrom carries an Error type for conversions that can fail; AsRef is a cheap view, and Borrow additionally promises identical Eq, Ord and Hash.
recipes.how: `impl From<f64> for Meters` lets call sites write `Meters::from(x)` or `x.into()`, and parameters take `impl Into<Meters>`. For checked construction write `impl TryFrom<f64> for UnitInterval { type Error = f64; fn try_from(v: f64) -> Result<Self, f64> { if (0.0..=1.0).contains(&v) { Ok(Self(v)) } else { Err(v) } } }`; the range test also rejects NaN. `u8::try_from(300u32)` is `Err` where `300u32 as u8` silently gives 44. `HashMap<String, V>::get("key")` works because String: Borrow<str> hashes and compares like str. Accept `impl AsRef<str>` or `impl AsRef<[f64]>` when a function only needs to read.
recipes.gotchas: From must not fail or lose information; a fallible or lossy From (e.g. f64 to an integer id) breaks its contract, use TryFrom. Do not implement Borrow for a wrapper whose Eq or Hash differ from the inner type's (std's CaseInsensitiveString example); AsRef is the safe choice there. When bounding a generic parameter, prefer `T: TryInto<U>` over `U: TryFrom<T>` (std's advice), and implement only From/TryFrom yourself: the API guidelines say never implement Into or TryInto.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs `signature` turns raw ABI values into refusals by returning None (NaN via `bad`, non-positive half-extents, counts over MAX_BODIES or MAX_COLLIDERS). A `TryFrom<f64>` newtype such as a positive half-extent is the trait-shaped version of that check, done once at the boundary; the #[repr(u8)] mode enum with TryFrom<u32> is types-patterns' hook.

recipes.what: Each operator is a std::ops trait impl with an Output type, and the binary operators take their operands by value, so a vector type must be Copy (or implement the ops for references) to be used again after `a + b`.

recipes.name: Satisfy the orphan rule with a local newtype and forward its methods; Deref does not confer trait impls
recipes.what: You may implement a trait only when the trait or the type is local to your crate (E0117 otherwise); a one-field wrapper struct makes the type local at no run-time cost, but Deref on that wrapper only forwards method calls and does not make the wrapper implement the inner type's traits.
recipes.how: `struct Samples(Vec<f64>); impl fmt::Display for Samples { .. }` compiles where `impl Display for Vec<f64>` is E0117 ('only traits defined in the current crate can be implemented for types defined outside of the crate'; rustc suggests a new trait or new type). The same holds for Rapier: `impl Hash for rapier3d_f64::math::Vector` is E0117, while `struct Key3(Vector)` with a to_bits Hash compiles. Give the wrapper the few methods it needs by delegation (`fn len(&self) -> usize { self.0.len() }`) or define a local trait. With `impl Deref<Target = Cube> for Tagged`, `tagged.volume()` resolves through auto-deref, yet `total(&[tagged])` with `T: Solid` is E0277.
recipes.gotchas: The Book itself offers Deref as a way to give a wrapper every method of the inner value; std's Deref page says not to implement it when methods may collide with the target's or when deref coercion should not become public API, and the API guidelines reserve Deref for smart pointers. The practical failure is the trait-bound gap: generic code sees the wrapper, not the target. A newtype also loses Debug, Clone, PartialEq and the rest; derive or forward each one.
recipes.engine_note: Rapier's `Vector` (glam DVec3) and `ColliderHandle` are foreign to si-solver, so any Hash, Ord or Display the law needs on them goes through a local wrapper or a local function. That is what the solver already does: `mix_f64` hashes components one by one, and the pair sort uses `into_raw_parts()` tuples.

recipes.name: Implement Iterator for your own type with type Item and next(); the adapters and for loops come free
recipes.what: Iterator has one required method, `next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>`; map, filter, zip, sum, collect and for-loop support all come from its provided methods and std's blanket IntoIterator impl.
recipes.how: Keep the cursor state in a struct and implement next: return `Some(item)` and advance, or `None` when done. Example: `impl<'a> Iterator for Rows<'a> { type Item = &'a [f64]; fn next(&mut self) -> Option<&'a [f64]> { .. } }` over a flat stride-17 buffer then works in `for r in rows`, `.map(|r| r[0]).collect::<Vec<_>>()` and `.filter(..).count()`. Override `size_hint` when the length is known (the default is (0, None)); call `.fuse()` or implement FusedIterator if callers rely on None staying None.

After next returns None a plain Iterator may resume (the fuse check shows Some, None, Some); `.fuse()` pins None. size_hint is advisory, and unsafe code must not trust it to skip bounds checks. Iterators are lazy: `v.iter().map(f);` with no consumer does nothing and rustc warns (`unused_must_use`: 'iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed'). Before writing one, check std: fixed-stride rows are what `slice::chunks_exact` (1.31+) already yields, as the run check confirms (collections lane).

recipes.name: Pick named-field, tuple or unit structs by meaning; hang constructors and constants on impl blocks
recipes.what: Rust has three struct kinds (named-field, tuple, unit-like); every fn in an impl block is an associated function, only those taking self are methods, and an associated const is evaluated only when something references it.
recipes.how: Named fields when fields have distinct roles (`struct Face { axis, pen, dir }`); a tuple struct for a one-field wrapper or a same-shaped but different type (`struct Quanta(u32)`); a unit-like struct (`struct Warm;`) for a type with no data. Constructors are associated functions returning `Self` (`fn new(x: f64, y: f64, z: f64) -> Self { Self { x, y, z } }`), fixed values are associated consts (`const ZERO: Vec3 = ...;`), both called through the type: `Vec3::new(..)`, `Vec3::ZERO`, `Self::PER_SECOND`. A type may have several impl blocks. Calling a self-less fn with method syntax (`v.new(..)`) is E0599 'this is an associated function, not a method'.
recipes.gotchas: An associated const is const-evaluated only when referenced, so `const CHECK: () = assert!(Self::MAX_BODIES <= 32);` inside an impl proves nothing until code names `Self::CHECK`; unreferenced, the false assertion compiles with only a dead_code warning ('associated constant `CHECK` is never used'), referenced it is E0080. Tuple-struct fields are positional (`.0`), so a tuple struct with several fields of one type invites transposition; use named fields there. Field-init shorthand and `..base` update syntax are conveniences, not further struct kinds.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs builds `Loaded.signature` by copying `Signature` field by field and compares signatures field by field in `same_sig`. `Signature` is a named-field struct of u32/u64 only (the f64 `cell` is stored as `to_bits()`), so derived Clone/Copy/PartialEq/Eq (contracts: traits-generics lane) could replace both hand-written copies. The slot numbers (`HX`..`DRIVEN` in lib.rs, `QX`..`WZ` in rapier_law.rs) are free consts; associated consts on a record type would namespace them without touching the ABI.

recipes.name: Model a closed set of body states as an enum with per-variant data, not a flag number or parallel vectors
recipes.what: An enum value is exactly one variant and carries only that variant's data, so the states a flag number or parallel Vec<bool> / Vec<Option<_>> admit but nobody means (mode 4.0, mode 1.5, NaN, kinematic with no handle) cannot be constructed.
recipes.how: Write `enum Slot { Carried, Dynamic { handle: RigidBodyHandle }, Kinematic { handle: RigidBodyHandle, lifted: bool } }` rather than a number compared with `== 1.0` or `kinematic: Vec<bool>` beside `handles: Vec<Option<_>>`. Data lives in the variant that needs it — building `Slot::Kinematic { lifted: true }` without its handle is E0063. Read it with an exhaustive `match`. A fieldless enum casts to its integer (`Mode::Lifted as u32` is 2); there is no integer-to-enum cast (`2u32 as Mode` is E0605), so numbers enter through `TryFrom` (ABI-edge recipe).
recipes.gotchas: A `bool` field or parameter is a two-variant flag with no name for a third state; the API guidelines (C-CUSTOM-TYPE) prefer a custom type because it can grow a variant. Explicit discriminants (`Dynamic = 0`) are allowed on unit-only enums or under a primitive representation such as #[repr(u8)]; they document the wire value but validate nothing coming in. Swapping a flag for an enum inside Rust leaves the ABI alone as long as the conversion happens at the export edge.

recipes.name: List every variant in a match: a `_` arm silently absorbs variants added later
recipes.what: match must be exhaustive (E0004 names the missing pattern), which turns 'a variant was added' into a compile error at every match that has to decide about it; a `_` arm switches that off and hands the new variant the default.
recipes.how: For enums you own, name every variant and leave `_` out, so adding `Carried` breaks each match until someone decides what Carried does. Use `_` (or a named catch-all such as `other`) for open domains (integers, floats, strings) and for #[non_exhaustive] enums from another crate, where the compiler requires it (std's `IntErrorKind`). Put a catch-all last: arms after it are unreachable and rustc warns (`unreachable_patterns`). A catch-all written as a named binding (`other => ..`) is just as silent as `_`.

recipes.name: Keep patterns edition-2024 clean: no `mut`, `ref` or `&` inside an implicitly borrowing pattern
recipes.what: Matching a reference with a non-reference pattern switches the default binding mode to ref / ref mut; Rust 2024 makes `mut`, `ref`, `ref mut`, `&` and `&mut` under that implicit mode hard errors, where Rust 2021 accepted them and a `mut` silently reset the binding to a by-value copy.
recipes.how: Either let match ergonomics bind (`let (a, b) = pair;` with `pair: &(u8, u8)` gives `a: &u8, b: &u8`) or make the prefix explicit (`let &(mut a, ref b) = pair;`); do not mix them. Before a 2021 crate changes edition, turn on the allow-by-default lint `#![warn(rust_2024_incompatible_pat)]`; `cargo fix --edition` applies its rewrites (`let [x, mut y] = &[(), ()];` becomes `let &[ref x, mut y] = &[(), ()];`). The three 2024 errors carry no error code: 'cannot mutably bind by value within an implicitly-borrowing pattern', 'cannot explicitly borrow within an implicitly-borrowing pattern', 'cannot explicitly dereference within an implicitly-borrowing pattern'.
recipes.rust_version: edition 2024 (errors); the lint runs in edition 2021 on 1.98.1
recipes.gotchas: The 2021 trap is `mut`: in `let (mut a, b) = &(1u8, 2u8);` `a` is a by-value u8 copy while `b` is `&u8`, so `a += 10` never touches the tuple. A redundant `ref` was harmless in 2021 and is an error in 2024, so code that compiled for years stops compiling on the edition bump. Edition is per crate: a 2021 crate keeps 2021 pattern rules on the 1.98.1 compiler.

recipes.name: Flatten refutable matches with let-else (1.65+); let chains need edition 2024; if-let guards work since 1.95
recipes.what: let-else (1.65, every edition) binds on match and makes the else block diverge; let chains (`if let .. && let ..`, 1.88) are edition-2024 only; if-let guards on match arms (1.95) work in every edition but never count toward exhaustiveness.
recipes.how: Early exits: `let Some(sig) = signature(..) else { return 0; };` — the else block must diverge (return, break, continue, panic), otherwise E0308 '`else` clause of `let...else` does not diverge'. Drain loops: `while let Some(x) = stack.pop() { .. }`. In edition 2024, chain with `&&` only: `if let Some(inner) = outer && let Some(n) = inner && n == 1 { .. }`; a bare `||` is rejected ('`||` operators are not supported in let chain conditions'), so parenthesise a `||` sub-expression. recipes.name: Use slice, @, range and array patterns (and matches!) instead of index arithmetic and comparison chains
recipes.what: Patterns test and bind in one step: `matches!(x, pat if guard)` yields a bool, `[head, tail @ ..]` splits a slice, `d @ 1..=9` binds the value it tested, exclusive `a..b` ranges are stable since 1.80, and an array pattern over `[f64; 17]` must name exactly 17 elements (E0527 otherwise).
recipes.how: `matches!(mode, Mode::Kinematic | Mode::Lifted)` (1.42) instead of `m == 1.0 || m == 2.0`; `[first, .., last]` and `[start @ .., last]` instead of length checks and indexing; ranges `a..=b`, `a..b`, `a..`, `..b`, `..=b` for numeric and char types only; integer ranges that together cover the type need no `_`. Empty ranges are compile errors (`10..=0` E0030, `10..10` E0579), and the warn-by-default lints `non_contiguous_range_endpoints` (`0..10` then `11..20` skips 10) and `overlapping_range_endpoints` (`0..=10` then `10..=20`) catch off-by-one bands. Float literals and float ranges are allowed in patterns (a NaN range endpoint is not), and a float match always needs `_` (E0004).

recipes.gotchas: Measured on 1.98.1: a float literal arm `0.0 =>` also takes -0.0 and NaN reaches only `_`, so a float match cannot tell signed zeros apart and can never be exhaustive by listing values. Inside a slice pattern a half-open range must be parenthesised (`[(a..), ..]`), and `name @ ..` is allowed only in slice patterns. `matches!` takes the same pattern syntax as a match arm, including `|` and an `if` guard.

recipes.name: Chain Option and Result with map, and_then, filter, ok_or_else and ?; convert between them explicitly
recipes.what: Option<T> and Result<T, E> are plain enums whose combinators and `?` replace nested matches; `?` works on Option only in a function returning Option and on Result only in one returning Result, so crossing needs ok_or / ok_or_else / .ok().
recipes.how: `x.map(f)` transforms the Some/Ok value; `x.and_then(f)` chains a step that can itself fail; `opt.filter(p)` drops values that fail a test; inside a Result fn, `opt.ok_or_else(|| err)?` turns None into an error; `res.ok()` drops the error; `opt.is_some_and(p)` (1.70), `opt.is_none_or(p)` (1.82), `Result::flatten` (1.89). `?` on None returns None; `?` on Err(e) returns Err(From::from(e)). Using `?` on an Option in a Result fn is E0277 ('the `?` operator can only be used on `Result`s, not `Option`s, in a function that returns `Result`'), and rustc suggests `.ok_or(...)?`.
recipes.gotchas: Arguments to ok_or, unwrap_or, map_or and or are evaluated eagerly even on the path that ignores them; std recommends the lazy _else forms when the argument is a function call. `Option<T>` is not `T`: the compiler refuses to use it as the value until it is matched or converted, which is the point. How the error type behind `?` should be designed belongs to the errors-panics lane.
recipes.engine_note: rapier_law.rs already uses `?` on Option in `quat_from_body` (`let (x, y, z, w) = canon_quat(..)?;`). In `build_world`, which returns Option too, `let Some((qx, qy, qz, qw)) = canon_quat(c[6], c[7], c[8], c[9]) else { return None; };` is equivalent to `let (qx, qy, qz, qw) = canon_quat(c[6], c[7], c[8], c[9])?;`. `solver_load` returns `if ensure(..) { 1 } else { 0 }`; `u32::from(ensure(..))` is the same conversion (From<bool> for integers, 1.28).

recipes.name: Wrap units and ids in tuple-struct newtypes; keep type aliases for renames and long names
recipes.what: A newtype (`struct Quanta(u32)`) is a distinct type the compiler keeps apart (E0308 on a mix-up); a type alias (`type Quanta = u32`) is only another name, so aliased values interconvert with no error.
recipes.how: Declare `#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)] struct BodyIndex(usize);`, `struct Quanta(u32);`, `struct Rows(u32); struct Cols(u32);` and convert at named points (`impl Quanta { fn seconds(self, dt: f64) -> f64 }`). Keep the field private where an invariant must hold and construct through `new` or `TryFrom`. Use `type` to shorten a long type or to keep an old name alive: rapier3d-f64 0.35.3 still exports `pub type BodyStatus = RigidBodyType;`, deprecated with 'renamed as RigidBodyType', and the two names assign to each other freely. An alias of a tuple struct is not its constructor (`type Q = Quanta; Q(32)` is E0423).
recipes.gotchas: Aliases document but do not protect: with `type Seconds = f64; type Quanta = f64;` a seconds value passes a quanta parameter silently. A newtype starts with none of the inner type's operators or trait impls (`Quanta(1) + Quanta(2)` is E0369) until you derive or implement them (ops traits and the orphan-rule workaround: traits-generics lane). Keep the extern "C" signature in plain u32/f64 and wrap on entry; layout attributes for passing wrappers across the boundary belong to the memory-layout lane.

recipes.name: Treat `as` as silent truncation or saturation; convert integers with From or TryFrom so a loss is visible
recipes.what: `as` never fails: narrowing keeps the low bits, float-to-int rounds toward zero and saturates (NaN -> 0), int-to-float rounds to nearest; std implements From only where no value can be lost and TryFrom returns Err instead of a wrong number.
recipes.how: Widen with From: `u64::from(x_u32)`, `f64::from(x_u32)` (exact), `usize::from(x_u16)`. Narrow or change sign with TryFrom: `u8::try_from(n)?`, `usize::try_from(n_u32)` — std has no `From<u32> for usize` (E0277), only `TryFrom<u32>` (the Reference guarantees usize at least 16 bits, not 32), and f64 has no `From<u64>` or `From<usize>`. Integer to bool: `bool::try_from(n)` (1.95; 0 and 1 only) — `7u8 as bool` is E0054. Keep `as` for intended bit reinterpretation (`-1i32 as u32` is 4294967295), deliberate truncation, or a saturating clamp, and say which in a comment.

Casts are not transitive: `e as U1 as U2` being valid does not make `e as U2` valid (Rustonomicon). Before 1.45 an out-of-range float-to-int cast was undefined behaviour (background source).

recipes.name: At the raw extern "C" edge, bounds-check counts and TryFrom each mode number into an enum; refuse the rest
recipes.what: Keep the flat f64/u32 ABI, but turn each raw number into a checked Rust value at the top of the export — counts compared with capacity before they become indices, mode numbers decoded through TryFrom into an enum — and return the export's failure code for anything else.
recipes.how: `#[repr(u8)] enum SolverMode { Dynamic = 0, Kinematic = 1, Lifted = 2, Carried = 3 }` plus `impl TryFrom<u32> for SolverMode` with an exhaustive `match` ending in `other => Err(other)`. Slot 16 is an f64, so decode it as `let n = x as u32; if f64::from(n) != x { refuse }` and then `SolverMode::try_from(n)`: the exact round trip refuses 1.5, -1.0, NaN and 1e10, which `x as u32` alone would turn into 1, 0, 0 and 4294967295. Going out, `mode as u32` is a defined enum cast. For counts, keep `if n_bodies as usize > MAX_BODIES { return 0; }` ahead of every loop that indexes `i * BODY_STRIDE + k`.
recipes.rust_version: any (checked on 1.98.1, host and wasm32-unknown-unknown, edition 2021 like the solver)
recipes.gotchas: `SolverMode::try_from(x as u32)` looks checked but inherits the cast's truncation and saturation (1.5 becomes Kinematic, NaN becomes Dynamic). -0.0 decodes to Dynamic because -0.0 == 0.0. Never transmute a number into an enum (invalid discriminants: unsafe-ffi lane). `u32 as usize` is lossless on wasm32 (usize is 32 bits) and on 64-bit hosts, so the cast is not the hazard; the index is: without the capacity check, body 64 reads index 1,088 of a 1,088-element array and panics inside the export (what a panic does under `panic = "abort"`: errors-panics lane).
recipes.engine_note: lib.rs `step()` and rapier_law.rs `signature()` both test `n_bodies as usize > MAX_BODIES` first (e5fbcb9). That test also guards the u64 masks: `signature()` sets `driven |= 1u64 << i` and `carried |= 1u64 << i`, sound only while MAX_BODIES <= 64. With the solver's release settings (`overflow-checks = false`, opt-level 3), `1u64 << 64` evaluates to 1 on the host and on wasm32 (measured), so raising MAX_BODIES without widening the masks would alias body 64 onto body 0 with no error. T2's `solver_restore(world_id, n_bodies, n_colliders, rows, cols, cell, shape, len)` (docs/dispatch-t2-restore.md) adds a byte length and must compare the snapshot's pair and point counts, which `rebuild_snapshot` writes as f64 (`pairs.len() as f64`, `n_points as f64`): bound `len` by the restore buffer before slicing and decode each stored count with the same exact round trip before comparing or using it. `shape: u32` (1 = capsule, any other value = cuboid today) is the next candidate for TryFrom decoding.
